track.tagline: Package an application with everything it needs and run it as an isolated container anywhere.
what: Docker is the standard tool for containers. It packs an application, its libraries and settings into an image, and runs copies of that image as containers that behave the same on a laptop, a test server or the cloud.
This track goes from the first `docker run` to writing your own images and running a multi-container stack with Compose.
how: An image is a read-only template built in layers from a Dockerfile; a container is a running copy with its own small writable layer. The Docker engine runs containers; the `docker` CLI talks to it.

Ports are published from host to container, volumes keep data beyond a container's life, and user-defined networks let containers find each other by name. Compose describes a whole stack in one YAML file.
track.who: Developers, students and operations engineers starting with containers; the base for Kubernetes.
learn: Tell images from containers and manage their lifecycle
Publish ports and understand host port conflicts
Keep data in named volumes
Connect containers by name on a user-defined network
Write a Dockerfile that uses the layer cache well
Describe and run a stack with Docker Compose
before: What a process, a port and a file path are
track.simulated: The Docker engine is simulated: commands create, start and inspect modelled images, containers, volumes and networks with Docker's real output and errors, without running real software.

terms.short: A packaged app with everything it needs, running isolated on a shared operating system - lighter than a virtual machine.
explain: An app needs the right libraries and settings to run. A container image bundles the app with all of them. Starting that image gives a container: an isolated process with its own files and network, but sharing the host's operating system kernel.

Because there is no separate operating system to boot, a container starts in a second and uses little memory. The same image runs the same way on a laptop and on a server. Docker made containers popular; Kubernetes runs many of them.
terms.example: `docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx` starts a web server container from the `nginx` image and connects host port 8080 to it.
terms.analogy: A shipping container: whatever is inside, it is loaded, moved and stacked the same way on any ship or truck.

terms.short: A tool that packages an application with everything it needs into an image, and runs it as an isolated container on any machine.
explain: 'It works on my machine' happens because servers differ: another library version, another setting. Docker solves this by packing the app, its libraries and its settings into one image. The image runs the same on a laptop, a test server or the cloud.

A running copy of an image is a container: an isolated process with its own filesystem and network, sharing the host's operating system kernel, so it starts in a second and uses little memory. The Docker daemon (engine) does the work; the `docker` command talks to it.
terms.example: `docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx` downloads the nginx image and runs it as a container called web.
terms.analogy: Shipping containers: whatever is inside, every crane and ship handles the box the same way.
terms.why: The Docker and data infrastructure labs build images and run containers on a simulated Docker engine.

terms.short: A read-only package containing an application and its files, built in layers, from which containers are started.
explain: An image is a template. It holds a filesystem - an operating system base, libraries, your code - and metadata such as which command to run. It never changes; each container gets a thin writable layer on top.

Images are named `repository:tag`, for example `python:3.12-slim` or `shopflow-ingest:2.0`. They are stored in a registry such as Docker Hub; `docker pull` downloads one. `docker history` shows the layers and how big each is.
terms.example: `docker pull nginx:1.27`, then `docker images` lists it with its size.

terms.short: A text file of instructions - start FROM this base, COPY these files, RUN this command - that Docker follows to build an image.
explain: Each line is an instruction: `FROM python:3.12-slim` picks the base image, `WORKDIR /app` sets the folder, `COPY requirements.txt .` copies files from the build context, `RUN pip install -r requirements.txt` runs a command, `CMD ["python","main.py"]` sets what runs at start.
The build context is the folder sent to the builder; `.dockerignore` keeps secrets and junk out of it. `docker build -t myapp:1.0 .` builds and tags the image.
terms.example: FROM, WORKDIR, COPY requirements, RUN pip install, COPY source, CMD - in that order so dependencies stay cached.

terms.short: Mapping a port on the host machine to a port inside a container (`-p 8080:80`), so programs outside can reach the containerised service.
explain: A container's ports are private to it. `-p 8080:80` means: traffic arriving at the host's port 8080 is forwarded to port 80 in the container. The host side comes first.
Only one program can listen on a host port, so a second container cannot also publish 8080 - it must use 8081. Inside the container both can still use port 80.
terms.example: `docker run -d -p 8080:80 --name web1 nginx` and `docker run -d -p 8081:80 --name web2 nginx`

terms.short: Storage managed by Docker that lives outside a container, so data survives when the container is removed or replaced.
explain: A container's own filesystem disappears when the container is removed. For a database that would lose everything. A volume is a separate storage area mounted into the container at a path, such as `/var/lib/postgresql/data`.
A named volume (`-v pgdata:/var/lib/...`) has a name you can reuse; an anonymous one gets a random id and is easy to lose. A volume cannot be removed while a container uses it.
terms.example: `docker volume create pgdata`, run postgres with `-v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data`, remove it, start a new one: the data is still there.

terms.short: A virtual network that connects containers; on a network you create, containers can find each other by name.
explain: Containers get their own IP addresses on a virtual network. On the default bridge network they can reach each other only by IP, which changes every time. On a network you create (`docker network create shop`), Docker runs a small DNS so a container can reach another simply by its name, like `db`.
A container can be on several networks at once. `docker inspect` shows its networks and addresses.
terms.example: `docker network create shop`, `docker network connect shop api`, then from api: `ping db` works.

terms.short: A tool that starts a set of related containers - an app, its database, its cache - from one YAML file with one command.
explain: Real apps are several containers. Writing a `docker run` line for each is error-prone. A compose file lists the services, their images, ports, environment variables, volumes and networks; `docker compose up -d` starts them all on a shared network where each service name is a hostname.

`depends_on` only orders start-up; with `condition: service_healthy` it also waits for a healthcheck. `${VAR:?}` makes a missing variable an error, `.env` supplies values, profiles start optional services, and `down` removes containers but keeps named volumes.
terms.example: A compose file with `web`, `api` and `db`; the api connects to `db:5432` by name.

terms.short: A program that is currently running; each one has a number called a process ID (PID).
explain: A program on disk is just a file. When you start it, the operating system loads it into memory and it becomes a process, with its own PID, memory and owner. One program can run as many processes at once.

`ps` lists your processes, `top` shows them live with their CPU and memory use, and `kill PID` asks one to stop (`kill -9` forces it). A command can also be limited in time, so a runaway loop does not run forever.
terms.example: In the processes lab, `ps` lists what you are running and a bounded command such as `timeout 2 sleep 10` stops itself after two seconds.
terms.analogy: A recipe is the program; actually cooking it in the kitchen right now is the process.

terms.short: A text window where you type commands to a computer and read what it prints back.
explain: A terminal is the window; it shows text and sends your keystrokes. Inside it runs a shell, the program that reads your command, runs it, and shows the output. People often say terminal, console and command line for the same thing.

In these labs the terminal is a tool beside the others, working on the same files. You type a command after the prompt (such as `student@lab:~$`) and press Enter. Up arrow repeats an earlier command; Tab completes names.
terms.example: Open the Linux Terminal, type `pwd` and press Enter: the shell prints the directory you are in.
terms.analogy: A chat window with the computer: you write a message (a command) and it writes back.

terms.short: One instruction typed into a terminal: a program name, followed by options and arguments.
explain: A command has a shape: `program subcommand --option value argument`. In `ls -la practice`, `ls` is the program, `-la` are flags (options), and `practice` is the argument it works on. Spaces separate the parts, so a name with a space needs quotes.
When a command finishes it returns an exit code: 0 means success, anything else means an error. Scripts and pipelines check that code to decide what to do next.
terms.example: `git commit -m "First commit"`: the program is `git`, the subcommand `commit`, the flag `-m`, and the quoted message is its value.

terms.short: A way of using a program by typing text commands instead of clicking buttons.
explain: A command-line interface (CLI) reads a line you type, does it, and prints the result as text. `git status`, `kubectl get pods` and `python manage.py migrate` are all CLI commands: a program name, then words and flags telling it what to do.

A CLI looks harder than a graphical interface at first, but it is faster for experts, it can be written into scripts, and it does exactly the same in every environment. Many cloud products offer both a portal and a CLI that call the same API.
terms.example: In the Django labs, `python manage.py makemigrations` is Django's CLI: no window opens, it reads your models and prints which migration it created.
terms.analogy: Giving instructions to an assistant in short exact sentences instead of pointing at things.

terms.short: A project folder tracked by version control, together with its whole history of commits.
explain: `git init` turns a folder into a repository by creating a hidden `.git` directory. That directory holds every commit, branch and tag; the files you see are just the working tree - the currently checked-out version.
A repository can live on your laptop (local) and on a server such as GitHub (remote). `git clone URL` copies a remote repository with its full history; `push` and `pull` keep the two in step.
terms.example: In the CS471 labs, the `cs471-labs` folder is one repository holding every lab, pushed to GitHub after each one.

terms.short: A desktop application for Windows and Mac that runs the Docker engine and shows containers, images and volumes in a window.
explain: On Linux Docker runs directly. On Windows and Mac, Docker Desktop provides a small Linux virtual machine with the engine inside, plus a graphical dashboard.
The dashboard lists containers with their status and ports, images with their sizes, and volumes - the same things `docker ps`, `docker images` and `docker volume ls` show.
terms.example: The image lab deletes the old 1.x images from Docker Desktop's Images view.

terms.short: A Linux command that prints only the lines of text that contain a word or pattern.
explain: `grep pattern file` reads the file line by line and prints each line that matches. Useful flags: `-i` ignores case, `-v` keeps lines that do NOT match, `-c` counts matches, `-n` shows line numbers, and `-r` searches every file in a directory tree.
The pattern can be a regular expression, a small language for text patterns, such as `^ERROR` (lines starting with ERROR). `grep` searches inside files; to find files by their name, use `find`.
terms.example: `grep -r "TODO" .` searches inside every file under the current directory for the word TODO.

terms.short: A graphical user interface: windows, buttons, menus and forms you use with a mouse or touch.
explain: A GUI shows information as pictures and controls. You click a button instead of typing a command, and you fill in a form instead of remembering flags. It is easier to discover, because the options are visible.

Behind the buttons, a GUI usually calls the same API or runs the same command a CLI would. Several labs here show both: a portal and a terminal working on the same objects, so you can see a click and the command it stands for.
terms.example: In the Git labs, GitHub Desktop is a GUI: pressing Commit to main runs the same `git commit` the terminal would.

terms.short: A free, open-source operating system that runs most of the world's servers, phones (Android) and cloud machines.
explain: Linux was started in 1991 by Linus Torvalds and is developed by thousands of people. Strictly, Linux is the kernel - the core that talks to the hardware - and a distribution such as Ubuntu adds the shell, tools and package manager around it.
On servers Linux is used mostly through a terminal, not a desktop. Everything is a file in one tree starting at `/`, programs are small tools that each do one job, and you combine them in the shell.
terms.example: The Linux labs give you a real shell in your own directory: `ls`, `cd`, `grep`, `chmod`, `tar` and pipes all behave as on a real Linux server.
terms.why: Docker, Kubernetes, the cloud and most servers run Linux, so these commands appear in almost every later lab.

terms.short: A complete pretend computer running as a program inside a real computer, with its own operating system.
explain: One powerful physical server can be split into many virtual machines (VMs). Special software called a hypervisor gives each VM a share of the real processor, memory and disk, and each one boots its own operating system.
To the software inside, a VM looks like a real machine. Clouds rent VMs by the minute. They are heavier than containers, because each VM carries a whole operating system.
terms.example: Renting a Linux VM in a cloud gives you a machine with an IP address you can log into with SSH, though no physical box was set up for you.
terms.analogy: Flats in one building: each has its own door, kitchen and furniture, but they share the same walls and foundations.

terms.short: The main program on a computer that manages the hardware and lets all other programs run.
explain: Programs do not talk to the hardware directly. They ask the operating system (OS): open this file, send this over the network, give me more memory. The OS shares the processor, memory and disk fairly between every running program.

The common operating systems are Windows (made by Microsoft), macOS (Apple), and Linux (free and open source). Almost every server on the internet runs Linux, which is why most labs here use Linux commands.
terms.example: When you type `ls` in a lab terminal, the shell asks the Linux operating system for the list of files in your directory, and the OS reads it from the disk.
terms.analogy: A building manager: tenants (programs) never fix the plumbing themselves; they ask the manager, who shares the building fairly.

terms.short: A way of working where developers and operations teams share responsibility and automate building, testing and releasing software.
explain: Traditionally developers wrote code and a separate operations team ran it on servers, and the hand-over was slow and full of blame. DevOps joins them: the same team builds, ships and runs the software.

It relies on automation: version control for everything, CI/CD pipelines that test and deploy every change, infrastructure written as code, containers, and monitoring. Small changes go out often, so problems are small and quick to fix.
terms.example: Pushing a commit triggers Jenkins to build, test and deploy the app - a DevOps pipeline replacing a manual release day.

terms.short: An open-source system that runs containers across a cluster of machines and keeps them running as described, restarting and moving them when needed.
explain: Docker runs containers on one machine. A real service needs many copies on many machines, restarts when one dies, rolling updates and load balancing. Kubernetes does that.

You describe the desired state in YAML - 'three copies of this image, reachable on port 80' - and send it to the cluster's API server. Controllers watch the actual state and keep fixing it until it matches. Nodes are the machines; Pods are the running units.
It was created at Google and is now maintained by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation. AKS, EKS and GKE are managed versions.
terms.example: `kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml` asks for three replicas; delete one Pod and Kubernetes starts a replacement.
terms.analogy: A shipping port's control tower: you say how many containers of each kind must be on the quay, and it moves cranes and ships to keep it so.

terms.short: Docker reuses already-built image layers when an instruction and its inputs have not changed, so ordering the Dockerfile well makes rebuilds fast.
explain: Every Dockerfile instruction makes a layer. When rebuilding, Docker checks each step: same instruction and same files as last time? Then it reuses the cached layer. The first step that changed, and every step after it, is rebuilt.
So copy what changes rarely first. Copy `requirements.txt` and install dependencies before copying your source; then a code change rebuilds only the last layer instead of reinstalling every package.
terms.example: With source copied before `pip install`, every code edit reinstalls all packages; swapped, the dependency layer stays CACHED.

terms.short: A Dockerfile with two or more FROM stages: one builds the app with compilers, the final one copies only the result, giving a small, safer image.
explain: Building often needs compilers and headers that the running app never uses. In a multi-stage build the first stage (`FROM python:3.12 AS builder`) installs and compiles; the last stage starts from a slim base and copies only the built packages.
The final image is smaller, faster to pull and has fewer tools an attacker could use. Adding `USER app` makes it run as a non-root user.
terms.example: The production image lab goes from 1.1 GB to about 150 MB, ships no compiler and runs as a non-root user.

terms.short: A number from 0 to 65535 that says which program on a computer should receive a piece of network traffic.
explain: One computer runs many network programs at once. The IP address gets data to the right computer; the port number gets it to the right program on that computer.

Well-known services use fixed ports: 80 for HTTP, 443 for HTTPS, 22 for SSH, 53 for DNS, 5432 for PostgreSQL. A program that waits for connections is said to listen on a port. Development servers often use 3000, 5000 or 8000.
terms.example: `http://localhost:5000` means: this same computer, port 5000 - which is where the Flask development server listens in the Flask labs.
terms.analogy: A flat number in an apartment building: the street address finds the building, the flat number finds the right door.

terms.short: A stable name and address in Kubernetes that forwards traffic to whichever Pods currently match its label selector.
explain: Pods come and go and change IP addresses. A Service gives one fixed name, like `web`, and a fixed virtual IP. It finds its Pods by labels (`app: web`) and spreads traffic over them; the matching Pod IPs are its endpoints.

A Service whose selector matches no Pod labels has no endpoints and silently goes nowhere - check `kubectl get endpoints`. ClusterIP is reachable only inside the cluster; NodePort also opens a port on every node.
terms.example: A Service with `selector: app: web` - from any Pod, `curl http://web` reaches one of the web Pods.

terms.short: A request by a Pod for durable storage of a certain size; Kubernetes binds it to a real disk that outlives the Pod.
explain: Container files vanish with the Pod. A PersistentVolumeClaim asks for, say, 1 GiB of storage. The cluster binds it to a PersistentVolume - an actual disk - and the Pod mounts the claim.

A Pod that refers to a claim that does not exist stays Pending; `kubectl describe pod` names the missing claim. StatefulSets create one claim per replica, and scaling down keeps the claims so the data is not lost.
terms.example: The Pod is Pending until `kubectl apply -f data-pvc.yaml` creates the claim it mounts.

terms.short: The internet's phone book: it turns a name like example.com into the IP address computers need.
explain: People remember names; computers need numbers. The Domain Name System (DNS) is a worldwide set of servers that answer one question: what is the IP address for this name?

Your computer asks a DNS resolver. If the resolver does not know, it asks the servers responsible for that domain, then caches the answer for a while. If DNS is broken, you can still reach a machine by its IP address but not by its name.
terms.example: In the networking lab a host can ping `192.168.10.20` but not `server.lab` until you add a DNS server with a record for that name.
terms.analogy: Looking up a friend's name in your phone's contacts to get the number you actually dial.

terms.short: A text format for data and settings that uses indentation instead of brackets, designed to be easy for people to read.
explain: YAML holds the same kind of data as JSON - names, values, lists - but writes it with spaces and dashes. `name: web` is a name and a value. A line starting with `- ` is a list item. Indentation shows what belongs inside what.
It is popular for configuration: Docker Compose, Kubernetes, Ansible and CI pipelines all use `.yml` files. The danger is indentation: one extra space changes the meaning, and tabs are not allowed.
terms.example: A tiny YAML file: `app:` then, indented two spaces, `port: 8000` and `debug: true`.
terms.analogy: An outline in a notebook, where how far you indent a line shows which heading it belongs to.

terms.short: A command or request run regularly to check a service is not just started but actually working; tools act on the result.
explain: A process can be running while it is useless - still starting, stuck, out of connections. A healthcheck asks a real question: does `pg_isready` succeed, does `GET /health` return 200?

Docker marks a container healthy or unhealthy, Compose can wait for healthy before starting dependants, load balancers stop sending traffic to unhealthy targets, and Kubernetes probes restart or bypass failing pods.
terms.example: `healthcheck: test: ["CMD", "pg_isready", "-U", "shop"] interval: 5s retries: 10`

terms.short: A number every command returns when it finishes: 0 means success, anything else means something went wrong.
explain: You do not always see whether a command worked, but the shell knows. Each command ends with an exit code. `echo $?` prints the code of the last command: `0` for success, `1`, `2`, `127` and so on for different failures.

Scripts and pipelines rely on this. `cmd1 && cmd2` runs `cmd2` only if `cmd1` succeeded; `if` in a shell script tests an exit code. CI tools such as Jenkins mark a stage failed when a command exits non-zero.
terms.example: `ls missing.txt; echo $?` prints an error and then `2`; `ls; echo $?` prints the listing and then `0`.

terms.short: The program inside a terminal that reads each command you type, runs it, and shows the result.
explain: The shell (on Linux usually `bash`) waits at a prompt. You type a line; it splits the line into a program name and arguments, finds that program, runs it, and prints what it outputs. Then it waits again.

The shell also adds powerful features: `|` pipes one command's output into another, `>` saves output to a file, `*` matches many file names, and `$NAME` uses a variable. A file of shell commands is a shell script.
terms.example: In `cat access.log | grep 404 | wc -l` the shell starts three programs and connects them, then prints the final count.
terms.analogy: An interpreter between you and the operating system: you speak in short commands, it passes them on and reports back.

terms.short: The most widely used version control tool: it records snapshots of a project's files so you can track and undo changes.
explain: Git was created in 2005 by Linus Torvalds, the creator of Linux. You run it in a project folder: `git init` starts tracking, `git add` chooses changes, `git commit` saves a snapshot, `git log` shows the history.

Every copy of a repository holds the full history, so you can work offline. Branches let you try ideas in parallel and merge them back. GitHub is a website that hosts Git repositories and adds collaboration features.
terms.example: In the first Git lab: `git init`, set your name with `git config`, write a file, `git add README.md`, `git commit -m "First commit"`, then `git log`.
terms.why: Every software team uses Git, and the CS471, Ansible and Jenkins labs push or read code from repositories.

terms.short: A saved snapshot of a project in version control, with a message, an author, and a link to the commit before it.
explain: `git commit -m "Add search form"` takes everything in the staging area and stores it as a new snapshot. Each commit records its author, time, message, and its parent commit, so the commits form a chain of history.

Each commit has a unique id, a hash such as `3f9a1c2`. A commit is a full snapshot, not a diff; Git computes the difference against the parent when you ask with `git show` or `git diff`. A merge commit has two parents.
terms.example: In the conflict lab, after resolving the merge you commit it and `git log --graph` shows a commit with two parents.

track.tagline: Addressing, VLANs, routing, services and ACLs in the Network Simulator.
what: Computer networking is how devices find and talk to each other: from two PCs on a switch to the whole internet. Network engineers design and fix these networks, and every cloud and DevOps role needs the basics.
This track uses the Network Simulator to build topologies, send packets, and read every layer of every packet - the kind of practice that normally needs a rack of Cisco equipment.
how: Each device has an IP address inside a subnet. Switches connect devices in one network using MAC addresses; VLANs split a switch into separate networks, and trunks carry several VLANs between switches.

Routers connect networks, choosing a path from their routing table, filled by static routes or by OSPF. Services complete the picture: DHCP hands out addresses, DNS turns names into addresses, NAT shares one public address, and ACLs decide what traffic may pass.
track.who: Students of networking (CCNA level), and developers and cloud engineers who need to understand addresses, subnets and routing.
learn: Address hosts and work out network, broadcast and host range by hand
Read a frame and a packet layer by layer
Segment a switch with VLANs and connect switches with a trunk
Configure static routes and OSPF and read a routing table
Configure DHCP, DNS and NAT
Write an ACL and prove the implicit deny
before: Know what an IP address is: see that glossary entry.
Comfort with binary numbers helps for subnetting, but the labs walk through it.
track.simulated: The network is simulated in the Network Simulator app: devices, packets and the IOS-style commands are modelled, not real hardware.

terms.short: A number that identifies a computer on a network, so data can be delivered to it.
explain: Every device on a network needs an address. An IPv4 address is four numbers from 0 to 255 separated by dots, such as `192.168.10.10`. IPv6 is a newer, much longer format with letters and colons.

Part of the address names the network and part names the device inside it; the subnet mask (the `/24` after the address) says where the split is. Addresses starting with `10.`, `172.16-31.` and `192.168.` are private: used inside homes and companies, never directly on the internet.
terms.example: In the networking lab you give two PCs `192.168.10.10/24` and `192.168.10.11/24`; because the first three numbers match, they are on the same network and can ping each other.
terms.analogy: A street address: the street name is the network part, the house number is the device part.

terms.short: A block of IP addresses that forms one network; the mask, such as /24, says how many leading bits are the network part.
explain: `192.168.10.10/24` means the first 24 bits (`192.168.10`) are the network and the last 8 bits are the host. The mask can also be written `255.255.255.0`. Hosts in the same subnet talk directly; to reach another subnet they go through a router.

Each subnet has a network address (first), a broadcast address (last) and usable host addresses between them. For `/26` the block size is 256 - 192 = 64, so `10.20.30.45/26` is in `10.20.30.0`-`.63`: network `.0`, broadcast `.63`, hosts `.1`-`.62`.
terms.example: The addressing lab breaks a ping on purpose by giving one host `/25` and the other `/24` - a mask mismatch, which is not symmetrical.

terms.short: A network device that connects computers in one local network and forwards each frame only to the port where its destination is.
explain: Plug several PCs into a switch and they form a local network (a LAN). The switch learns which device's MAC address is on which port by watching the frames that arrive, and keeps a MAC address table.

When a frame arrives, the switch looks up the destination MAC and sends it out of that one port; if it does not know yet, it floods the frame to all ports. A switch works at layer 2: it reads MAC addresses, not IP addresses. VLANs split one switch into several separate networks.
terms.example: The first networking lab builds two PCs and a switch; the ping works because the switch delivers the frames between them.

terms.short: A network device that connects different networks and forwards packets between them by their destination IP address.
explain: A switch connects devices inside one network; a router connects networks to each other - your home network to your internet provider, or one company VLAN to another. Each router interface has an IP address in the network it touches.

For each packet the router reads the destination IP, looks it up in its routing table, and sends it out of the best interface toward the next hop. A host sends anything not on its own network to its default gateway, which is a router.
terms.example: The routing lab builds three routers in a line; the two ends can reach each other only after the routers know routes to every network.

terms.short: The small unit in which data travels over a network, wrapped in layers of headers that carry addresses.
explain: Data is cut into pieces and wrapped like nested envelopes. The innermost is your data (an HTTP request). Around it a TCP or UDP header adds ports; an IP header adds source and destination IP addresses - that is a packet. An Ethernet header with MAC addresses around it makes a frame.

Each device reads the layer it cares about: a switch reads the frame's MACs, a router reads the packet's IP and lowers its TTL (time to live) by one - at zero the packet is dropped, which stops packets looping forever.
terms.example: In the networking labs you open one packet and read it layer by layer: Ethernet, then IPv4 with its TTL, then ICMP or TCP, then the data.
terms.analogy: A letter in an envelope inside a courier bag: each handler only reads the label on the layer they deal with.

terms.short: A virtual LAN: a way to split one physical switch into several separate networks that cannot see each other.
explain: Without VLANs every port on a switch is in one network. With VLANs you assign ports: ports 1-4 to VLAN 10 (staff), ports 5-8 to VLAN 20 (guests). Hosts in different VLANs cannot reach each other, even on the same switch.

This improves security and limits broadcasts. To let VLANs talk, traffic must be routed: a router, or a switch virtual interface (SVI) - an IP address for each VLAN on a layer-3 switch - acts as the gateway between them.
terms.example: In the VLAN lab you create two VLANs, prove the hosts cannot reach each other, then add SVIs and route between them.

terms.short: The list a router keeps of which networks it can reach and through which next hop or interface.
explain: Each entry says: to reach network `10.3.0.0/24`, send to next hop `10.0.12.2`. Directly connected networks appear automatically. Others are added by hand (static routes, `ip route 10.3.0.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.12.2`) or learned from a routing protocol such as OSPF.

When several entries match a destination, the most specific one (the longest prefix, e.g. /24 over /16) wins. If two sources offer the same prefix, the lower administrative distance wins: static 1 beats OSPF 110.
terms.example: In the routing lab you read a routing table and pick the longest match for a destination, then replace the static routes with OSPF.

terms.short: A program that imitates a real system so you can practise on it safely, without the cost or risk of the real thing.
explain: Some products cannot run inside a learning platform: a real cloud account costs money, a real network needs hardware. A simulation recreates how the product behaves - its commands, its objects, its error messages - in software.

Each lab tool says what is simulated and what is real. In a simulation the important behaviour is modelled carefully, but some rare features may be missing; if something seems different from the real product, the tool's note explains why.
terms.example: The Git tool simulates commits, branches and merges in Python with no remote, while the SQL editor is a real SQLite database.
terms.analogy: A flight simulator: pilots learn the controls and emergencies without leaving the ground.
terms.why: Many tools in these labs are simulations. Reading the tool's note tells you what to trust as real.

terms.short: A way of writing a range of IP addresses as one address plus a size, like `10.0.0.0/16`, used to size networks and subnets.
explain: Every machine on a network needs an IP address. When you build a cloud network you reserve a whole range at once. CIDR notation writes that range as a starting address and a slash number.

The number after the slash says how many leading bits are fixed. `/16` fixes 16 bits and leaves about 65,000 addresses; `/24` leaves 256. A subnet must sit inside its network's range, and two networks you want to connect must not overlap - Azure and AWS refuse overlapping ranges.
terms.analogy: Like a street with house numbers 1-256: the street is the network, and you hand out blocks of numbers to each building (subnet).

terms.short: A command that sends a small test packet to another host and waits for a reply, to check it is reachable.
explain: `ping 192.168.10.11` sends ICMP echo requests; the other host answers with echo replies. Each reply shows the round-trip time. No reply means something is wrong on the way: an address, a mask, a route, a firewall or an ACL.
`traceroute` (or `tracert`) builds on the same idea with increasing TTL values to list every router on the path. Ping is usually the first test in any network problem.
terms.example: The addressing lab gives both PCs a `/24` address and asks you to ping successfully - then breaks it with a mask mismatch.

terms.short: Address Resolution Protocol: how a computer finds the MAC address that belongs to an IP address on its local network.
explain: Before PC A can send a frame to `192.168.10.11`, it needs that host's MAC address. It broadcasts an ARP request to everyone: 'Who has 192.168.10.11?' The owner replies directly: 'That is me, my MAC is ...'.
PC A stores the answer in its ARP cache for a while, so the next packets go straight out. For an address on another network, ARP asks for the MAC of the default gateway instead.
terms.example: In the first networking lab, the packet trace shows an ARP request and reply just before the first ping goes out.

terms.short: A hardware address burned into each network card, like 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e, used to deliver frames inside a local network.
explain: Every network interface has a MAC address: six pairs of hexadecimal digits. Switches use it to deliver frames on the local network. IP addresses identify a device across networks; MAC addresses identify it on the wire right next to it.

To send to an IP on its own subnet, a computer must learn that device's MAC address, which it asks for with ARP. When a packet crosses a router, the MAC addresses change at each hop, while the IP addresses stay the same.
terms.example: Reading a ping in the packet trace shows two addresses per layer: source and destination MAC in the Ethernet header, source and destination IP inside.

terms.short: A Linux command that prints only the lines of text that contain a word or pattern.
explain: `grep pattern file` reads the file line by line and prints each line that matches. Useful flags: `-i` ignores case, `-v` keeps lines that do NOT match, `-c` counts matches, `-n` shows line numbers, and `-r` searches every file in a directory tree.
The pattern can be a regular expression, a small language for text patterns, such as `^ERROR` (lines starting with ERROR). `grep` searches inside files; to find files by their name, use `find`.
terms.example: `grep -r "TODO" .` searches inside every file under the current directory for the word TODO.

terms.short: A free, open-source operating system that runs most of the world's servers, phones (Android) and cloud machines.
explain: Linux was started in 1991 by Linus Torvalds and is developed by thousands of people. Strictly, Linux is the kernel - the core that talks to the hardware - and a distribution such as Ubuntu adds the shell, tools and package manager around it.
On servers Linux is used mostly through a terminal, not a desktop. Everything is a file in one tree starting at `/`, programs are small tools that each do one job, and you combine them in the shell.
terms.example: The Linux labs give you a real shell in your own directory: `ls`, `cd`, `grep`, `chmod`, `tar` and pipes all behave as on a real Linux server.
terms.why: Docker, Kubernetes, the cloud and most servers run Linux, so these commands appear in almost every later lab.

terms.short: A text window where you type commands to a computer and read what it prints back.
explain: A terminal is the window; it shows text and sends your keystrokes. Inside it runs a shell, the program that reads your command, runs it, and shows the output. People often say terminal, console and command line for the same thing.

In these labs the terminal is a tool beside the others, working on the same files. You type a command after the prompt (such as `student@lab:~$`) and press Enter. Up arrow repeats an earlier command; Tab completes names.
terms.example: Open the Linux Terminal, type `pwd` and press Enter: the shell prints the directory you are in.
terms.analogy: A chat window with the computer: you write a message (a command) and it writes back.

terms.short: The worldwide network that connects billions of computers so they can send data to each other.
explain: The internet is many smaller networks - homes, companies, universities, data centres - joined together by routers that pass data along. No single company owns it.

Data travels in small pieces called packets. Each packet carries the address of the computer it is going to (its IP address), and routers forward it hop by hop until it arrives. The web, email and video calls are all services that run on top of the internet.
terms.example: In the Wireshark lab, loading neverssl.com sends packets from the laptop through the home router out to the internet and back.
terms.analogy: The postal system: letters (packets) carry an address and are passed from sorting office to sorting office until they reach the door.

terms.short: The internet's phone book: it turns a name like example.com into the IP address computers need.
explain: People remember names; computers need numbers. The Domain Name System (DNS) is a worldwide set of servers that answer one question: what is the IP address for this name?

Your computer asks a DNS resolver. If the resolver does not know, it asks the servers responsible for that domain, then caches the answer for a while. If DNS is broken, you can still reach a machine by its IP address but not by its name.
terms.example: In the networking lab a host can ping `192.168.10.20` but not `server.lab` until you add a DNS server with a record for that name.
terms.analogy: Looking up a friend's name in your phone's contacts to get the number you actually dial.

terms.short: A number from 0 to 65535 that says which program on a computer should receive a piece of network traffic.
explain: One computer runs many network programs at once. The IP address gets data to the right computer; the port number gets it to the right program on that computer.

Well-known services use fixed ports: 80 for HTTP, 443 for HTTPS, 22 for SSH, 53 for DNS, 5432 for PostgreSQL. A program that waits for connections is said to listen on a port. Development servers often use 3000, 5000 or 8000.
terms.example: `http://localhost:5000` means: this same computer, port 5000 - which is where the Flask development server listens in the Flask labs.
terms.analogy: A flat number in an apartment building: the street address finds the building, the flat number finds the right door.

terms.short: Network Address Translation: a router rewriting private inside addresses into its public address as traffic leaves the network.
explain: Private addresses like `192.168.10.x` cannot be used on the internet. NAT on the edge router replaces the private source address of each outgoing packet with its own public address, and puts the original back on the replies.

With overload (PAT), many inside hosts share one public address, told apart by source port number. NAT is why a whole home or office can browse with one public IP - and why outside hosts cannot start connections inward by default.
terms.example: In the services lab you configure `ip nat inside source list 1 interface Gi0/1 overload` and compare a packet's source address and port on each side of the router.

terms.short: Transmission Control Protocol: a reliable way to send data, which numbers every byte, confirms delivery and re-sends what is lost.
explain: IP delivers packets but promises nothing: they can be lost, duplicated or arrive out of order. TCP runs on top and turns that into a reliable stream. It first opens a connection (the three-way handshake), numbers the data, and the receiver acknowledges what arrived.
Missing pieces are sent again and everything is put back in order. HTTP, HTTPS, SSH and database connections all use TCP. The cost is a little extra delay and overhead compared with UDP.
terms.example: Following the TCP stream of the web request in Lab 1 shows the whole HTTP conversation rebuilt from many TCP segments.

terms.short: A free program that captures the packets passing through a network card and shows every layer of each one.
explain: Wireshark records network traffic and lists each frame: time, source, destination, protocol and a summary. Click one and it dissects it layer by layer - Ethernet, IP, TCP, HTTP - with every header field explained, and the raw bytes below.

A busy network produces thousands of packets a second, so display filters narrow the list, and Follow TCP Stream rebuilds a whole conversation. It is the standard tool for learning protocols and for diagnosing network problems.
terms.example: In CS471 Lab 1 you capture on `wlan0` while browsing neverssl.com, filter with `http`, and open the GET request and its 200 response.

terms.short: A link between switches that carries traffic for many VLANs at once, tagging each frame with its VLAN number.
explain: Two switches each have VLAN 10 and VLAN 20. Instead of one cable per VLAN, a single trunk link carries them all. Each frame on the trunk gets a small 802.1Q tag that says which VLAN it belongs to.
The receiving switch reads the tag and delivers the frame only to ports in that VLAN, removing the tag. Ordinary ports to PCs are access ports: they belong to one VLAN and send untagged frames.
terms.example: In the VLAN lab you add a second switch and a trunk between them, then capture a tagged frame on the trunk and read its VLAN id.

terms.short: Open Shortest Path First: a routing protocol that lets routers discover each other and build their routing tables automatically.
explain: Static routes must be typed and updated by hand on every router. With OSPF, routers on the same links become neighbours, share what networks they have, and each computes the shortest path to every network.

When a link fails, the routers notice, share the change and recalculate - they reconverge - and traffic takes another path without anyone editing a route. OSPF routes appear in the routing table marked `O`, with administrative distance 110.
terms.example: In the routing lab you replace the static routes with OSPF, then break a link and watch OSPF find the path around it.

terms.short: A machine that follows instructions to store, change and show information.
explain: A computer has four main parts. The processor (CPU) follows instructions very fast. Memory (RAM) holds what it is working on right now. Storage (a disk) keeps files even when the power is off. The network card lets it talk to other computers.
A program is a list of instructions. When you run a program, the computer copies it from the disk into memory and the processor works through it, step by step, millions of times per second.
terms.example: Your laptop, your phone and the machines that run the websites in these labs are all computers - they differ in size, not in kind.
terms.analogy: A kitchen: the cook is the processor, the counter is memory, the pantry is the disk, and the recipe is the program.
terms.why: Every lab runs on computers you cannot see. Knowing the parts makes words like memory, disk and process make sense.

terms.short: A complete pretend computer running as a program inside a real computer, with its own operating system.
explain: One powerful physical server can be split into many virtual machines (VMs). Special software called a hypervisor gives each VM a share of the real processor, memory and disk, and each one boots its own operating system.
To the software inside, a VM looks like a real machine. Clouds rent VMs by the minute. They are heavier than containers, because each VM carries a whole operating system.
terms.example: Renting a Linux VM in a cloud gives you a machine with an IP address you can log into with SSH, though no physical box was set up for you.
terms.analogy: Flats in one building: each has its own door, kitchen and furniture, but they share the same walls and foundations.

terms.short: A Virtual Private Cloud: your own isolated private network inside AWS, where your servers and databases get their IP addresses.
explain: When you put servers in AWS they need a network. A VPC is that network: you give it an address range such as `10.0.0.0/16`, then divide it into subnets, add route tables saying where traffic goes, and gateways to reach the internet.

Nothing reaches a resource in your VPC from outside unless you open a path on purpose. Every account comes with a default VPC; real projects build their own. A VPC cannot be deleted while it still contains subnets or other resources.
terms.example: `aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.0.0.0/16` creates the network; subnets and security groups are then created inside it.
terms.analogy: A private office floor in a shared skyscraper: you decide the room layout, the locks, and which doors lead to the street.

terms.short: An Azure Virtual Network: a private network in Azure with an address range, divided into subnets, where VMs and services connect.
explain: A VNet is Azure's version of the AWS VPC. You give it an address space such as `10.10.0.0/16` and create subnets inside it. Resources in a VNet can talk to each other privately.

Some subnet names are special and required by Azure services: `AzureFirewallSubnet` for a firewall, `GatewaySubnet` for a VPN gateway. Separate VNets do not talk until you peer them, and peered ranges must not overlap.
terms.example: `az network vnet create --name vnet-hub --address-prefixes 10.0.0.0/16 --subnet-name AzureFirewallSubnet --subnet-prefixes 10.0.1.0/26`

terms.short: The delay between asking for something and starting to get the answer, usually measured in milliseconds.
explain: Every request takes time: the data travels over the network, waits in queues, and is processed. Latency is that wait. A web page with 50 ms latency feels instant; 2 seconds feels slow.

Distance, slow disks, too many round trips and busy servers all add latency. Caching, putting servers closer to users, indexes and fewer requests reduce it. Latency is different from bandwidth, which is how much data per second can flow.
terms.example: `ping` prints a time for each reply, such as `time=12 ms` - that is the round-trip latency to the other host.
terms.analogy: The time between pressing a doorbell and the door opening, regardless of how many people then walk out.

terms.short: The | symbol in a shell, which sends the output of one command straight into the next command as its input.
explain: Linux tools are small and each does one job: `grep` keeps matching lines, `sort` sorts, `uniq` removes repeats, `wc -l` counts lines. A pipe `|` connects them, so the text flows from one to the next without temporary files.

`cut -d' ' -f1 access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr` reads like a sentence: take the first field, sort it, count each value, sort by count, biggest first. Order matters - `uniq` only removes repeats that are next to each other, so `sort` must come first.
terms.example: `grep 404 access.log | wc -l` counts how many lines of the log mention 404 - a task in the text-processing lab.
terms.analogy: A factory line where each worker does one small job and passes the piece to the next.

terms.short: A Linux command that searches a directory tree for files by name, type, size or age.
explain: `find` walks a directory and everything below it, testing each entry against filters you give: `-name "*.txt"` for a name pattern, `-type f` for files only, `-type d` for directories only, `-size +1M`, `-mtime -1` for changed in the last day.

Filters combine, and each one narrows the result. Remember the split: `find` looks at file names and properties, `grep` looks inside files at their contents. Together - `find . -name "*.py" | xargs grep import` - they search a whole project.
terms.example: `find . -type d` lists only the directories under the current one; `find . -name "*.log"` finds every log file by name.

terms.short: A file or stream where a program writes a line for each thing that happens, with a time, so you can see what it did.
explain: Programs cannot show you what happened inside them unless they write it down. A log line usually has a timestamp, a level (INFO, WARNING, ERROR) and a message, for example `10:12:03 ERROR database not reachable`.
Web servers log every request; applications log errors. When something breaks, reading the log is usually the first step. Tools like `tail`, `grep` and log dashboards help find the lines that matter.
terms.example: In the Linux text lab you build a small access log and count the lines that mention 404 with `grep 404 access.log | wc -l`.
terms.analogy: A ship's logbook: each entry records the time and what happened, so problems can be traced later.

track.tagline: The three languages of every web page, with a live result pane.
what: Every website is built from three languages that browsers understand. HTML describes the structure: headings, paragraphs, links, images, forms. CSS describes the look: colours, spacing, layout. JavaScript adds behaviour: reacting to clicks, checking forms, fetching data.
This track teaches each one with a playground that renders your page as you type, the same way w3schools does. Django, Flask and Ionic pages all end up as these three languages in a browser.
how: The browser reads HTML and builds a tree of elements, the DOM. CSS rules select elements and style them; every element is a box with padding, border and margin, and flexbox and grid arrange the boxes.
JavaScript reads and changes the DOM, listens for events such as clicks and form submits, and talks to servers with `fetch`, using `async`/`await` to wait for the answer without freezing the page.
track.who: Anyone building or debugging web pages: front-end and full-stack developers, and back-end developers who need to write templates.
learn: Write well-formed HTML with correct nesting and alt text
Style elements with selectors and understand the box model
Lay out pages with flexbox and grid, responsive without breakpoints
Write modern JavaScript: const/let, arrow functions, map/filter/reduce
Change the page through the DOM and handle events
Build an accessible form and validate it
Fetch data from an API and handle loading, success and failure
before: Knowing what a URL and a web browser are helps; see those glossary entries.
track.simulated: Real: your own browser renders the HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a sandboxed frame; nothing is simulated.

terms.short: The program, such as Chrome, Firefox or Safari, that downloads web pages and shows them.
explain: A browser is an HTTP client and a page renderer. It sends a request for a URL, receives HTML, then fetches the CSS, JavaScript and images it mentions, builds the DOM, applies styles, runs scripts and paints the result.

Developer tools (F12) show the DOM, the CSS applied to each element, the console where errors appear, and the Network tab listing every request with its status code - the first places to look when a page misbehaves.
terms.example: The lab's Browser and Phone tools render your page in a sandboxed frame inside your own browser, just as a real visitor would see it.

terms.short: The language that describes the structure of a web page - headings, paragraphs, links, images - using tags.
explain:
HTML (HyperText Markup Language) marks up content with tags in angle brackets: `

Title

`, `

A paragraph.

`, `About`. Tags nest inside each other to form a tree, starting from ``, with `` and `` inside.
HTML says what things are, not how they look - that is CSS. Using the right tag (a heading, a list, a button) helps screen readers, search engines and every browser understand the page.
terms.example:
The first web lab asks for an `

`, a `

`, a list with `

  • `, a link with ``, and an `` with an `alt` attribute.
terms.why: Every web, Django, Flask and Ionic page in these labs ends up as HTML in a browser.

terms.short: The language that decides how a web page looks: colours, fonts, spacing and layout.
explain: CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) is a list of rules. Each rule has a selector (which elements) and declarations (what to change): `h1 { color: navy; font-size: 2rem; }`. The browser applies every matching rule to the HTML.

CSS can be inline (`style="..."` on one element), internal (a `<style>` block) or external (a `.css` file linked from the page - the usual way). When rules conflict, the more specific selector, or the later rule, wins: that is the cascade.
terms.example: In the CSS lab you style an element by tag name, add a class and style it, then give one element padding, margin and a border.

terms.short: The programming language that runs inside web browsers and makes pages interactive.
explain: HTML gives a page structure and CSS gives it style; JavaScript gives it behaviour. It reacts to clicks, checks forms, changes the page without reloading, and fetches data from servers. It also runs on servers through Node.js.

Modern JavaScript uses `const` for names that are not rebound and `let` for ones that are, arrow functions (`x => x * 2`), and array methods such as `map`, `filter` and `reduce` that return new arrays instead of changing the old one.
terms.example: `const prices = [5, 12, 20]; const big = prices.filter(p => p > 10);` - an arrow function used with filter, as the JavaScript lab asks.

terms.short: The Document Object Model: the browser's live tree of a page's elements, which JavaScript can read and change.
explain: When a browser loads HTML it builds a tree of objects, one per element: the DOM. JavaScript changes the page by changing this tree: `document.getElementById("total")` finds an element, and `el.textContent = "42"` changes its text instantly.

You can also create elements (`document.createElement("li")`) and add them (`list.append(li)`). Use `textContent` for text from users, not `innerHTML`: `innerHTML` treats text as HTML, so user input could inject a script.
terms.example: In the DOM lab you select an element by id, change its text with `textContent`, and append a new `<li>` you created.

terms.short: The set of rules browsers and servers use to ask for and send web pages and data.
explain: HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is a conversation of requests and responses. A request has a method (GET to read, POST to send data, PUT/PATCH to change, DELETE to remove), a path such as `/books/`, and headers.

The response starts with a status code: 200 means OK, 201 created, 301/302 moved, 404 not found, 405 method not allowed, 500 the server failed. Then come headers and the body - an HTML page, an image or JSON.
terms.example: In the Wireshark lab you open a `GET / HTTP/1.1` request and the `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` response that answered it, header by header.
terms.analogy: Ordering at a counter with a fixed form: tick what you want (method), write the item (path), and the reply comes back stamped OK or Not found.
terms.why: Every web, API and backend lab sends HTTP. Reading the method and status code is the fastest way to find what went wrong.

terms.short: The full address of something on the web, such as https://example.com/books/12/?name=ali.
explain: A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) has parts. The scheme (`https://`) says how to talk. The host (`example.com`) says which server. An optional port follows a colon. The path (`/books/12/`) says what you want on that server.

After a `?` comes the query string, `name=ali`, extra values for the server. After a `#` comes a fragment, used only by the browser. Web frameworks such as Django and Flask read the path to decide which code runs.
terms.example: In the Django labs `/books/index2/12/` routes to a view that receives `12` as a parameter, and `/books/?name=ali` passes `ali` in the query string.
terms.analogy: A full postal address: country, city, street, house, and a note for the person who opens the door.

terms.short: HTTP sent through an encrypted connection, so nobody in between can read or change it.
explain: Plain HTTP travels as readable text: anyone on the same Wi-Fi or along the route could see passwords or change the page. HTTPS wraps the same HTTP messages in TLS encryption.

When the connection starts, the server shows a certificate proving its name, and both sides agree on secret keys. After that every byte is encrypted. The browser shows a padlock. HTTPS normally uses port 443.
terms.example: The Wireshark lab browses `neverssl.com` precisely because it uses plain HTTP; on an HTTPS site the capture would show only encrypted bytes.
terms.analogy: Sending a letter in a locked box that only the receiver can open, instead of on a postcard anyone can read.

terms.short: One piece of a web page: an opening tag, content and closing tag, with attributes that add details, like Home.
explain: An element is `<tag>content</tag>`. Attributes go inside the opening tag as `name="value"`: `href` says where a link goes, `src` which image to load, `alt` a text description of an image, `id` and `class` give names for CSS and JavaScript.

Some elements are empty and have no closing tag, such as `` and `
`. Elements must nest properly: `

bold

`, never `

`. Headings go in order (`h1`, then `h2`), which tools use to build an outline.
terms.example: `` - an element whose `alt` attribute is read aloud when the image cannot be seen.

terms.short: Checking an HTML page against the official rules, for example with the W3C validator, to find mistakes browsers silently hide.
explain: Browsers are forgiving: a missing closing tag or a misspelled attribute usually still displays something, so errors go unnoticed. A validator reads the page and lists every rule broken, with line numbers.
The W3C Markup Validation Service is the standard one. Typical findings: unclosed elements, elements nested in the wrong place, duplicate `id`s, an `` without `alt`, or a missing ``.
terms.example: In CS471 Labs 4 and 5 you run one of your pages through the W3C validator and fix what it reports.

terms.short: A read-only package containing an application and its files, built in layers, from which containers are started.
explain: An image is a template. It holds a filesystem - an operating system base, libraries, your code - and metadata such as which command to run. It never changes; each container gets a thin writable layer on top.

Images are named `repository:tag`, for example `python:3.12-slim` or `shopflow-ingest:2.0`. They are stored in a registry such as Docker Hub; `docker pull` downloads one. `docker history` shows the layers and how big each is.
terms.example: `docker pull nginx:1.27`, then `docker images` lists it with its size.

terms.short: A Linux command that prints only the lines of text that contain a word or pattern.
explain: `grep pattern file` reads the file line by line and prints each line that matches. Useful flags: `-i` ignores case, `-v` keeps lines that do NOT match, `-c` counts matches, `-n` shows line numbers, and `-r` searches every file in a directory tree.
The pattern can be a regular expression, a small language for text patterns, such as `^ERROR` (lines starting with ERROR). `grep` searches inside files; to find files by their name, use `find`.
terms.example: `grep -r "TODO" .` searches inside every file under the current directory for the word TODO.

terms.short: A free, open-source operating system that runs most of the world's servers, phones (Android) and cloud machines.
explain: Linux was started in 1991 by Linus Torvalds and is developed by thousands of people. Strictly, Linux is the kernel - the core that talks to the hardware - and a distribution such as Ubuntu adds the shell, tools and package manager around it.
On servers Linux is used mostly through a terminal, not a desktop. Everything is a file in one tree starting at `/`, programs are small tools that each do one job, and you combine them in the shell.
terms.example: The Linux labs give you a real shell in your own directory: `ls`, `cd`, `grep`, `chmod`, `tar` and pipes all behave as on a real Linux server.
terms.why: Docker, Kubernetes, the cloud and most servers run Linux, so these commands appear in almost every later lab.

terms.short: A written language with strict rules that people use to give instructions to a computer.
explain: A computer only understands simple numeric instructions. A programming language lets people write instructions in words and symbols instead; a compiler or interpreter translates them for the machine.

Each language has its own grammar (syntax) and strengths: Python for scripts and data, JavaScript for web pages, SQL for databases, TypeScript for large web apps. Ideas such as variables, conditions, loops and functions appear in almost all of them.
terms.example: The web labs use three languages together: HTML for structure, CSS for style, and JavaScript - a programming language - for behaviour.

terms.short: A text window where you type commands to a computer and read what it prints back.
explain: A terminal is the window; it shows text and sends your keystrokes. Inside it runs a shell, the program that reads your command, runs it, and shows the output. People often say terminal, console and command line for the same thing.

In these labs the terminal is a tool beside the others, working on the same files. You type a command after the prompt (such as `student@lab:~$`) and press Enter. Up arrow repeats an earlier command; Tab completes names.
terms.example: Open the Linux Terminal, type `pwd` and press Enter: the shell prints the directory you are in.
terms.analogy: A chat window with the computer: you write a message (a command) and it writes back.

terms.short: A program that sends a request to a server and uses the answer it gets back.
explain: A client starts the conversation. Your web browser is a client: you type an address, it sends a request to a web server, and it shows the page that comes back.
Clients are not only browsers. The `git` command talking to GitHub, `curl` calling an API, and a phone app loading a list are all clients. One server usually serves many clients at the same time.
terms.example: In the Ionic full-stack lab the phone app is the client: it calls the Flask API (the server) and shows the rows it gets back.
terms.analogy: A customer in a restaurant: you ask for something, then wait for it to be brought to you.

terms.short: The part of a CSS rule that picks which elements it applies to, such as p, .card, #main or a:hover.
explain: A tag selector (`p`) picks every paragraph. A class selector (`.card`) picks elements with `class="card"`. An id selector (`#main`) picks the one element with `id="main"`. A descendant selector (`nav a`) picks links inside a nav.

Pseudo-classes pick a state: `a:hover` while the mouse is over a link, `a:visited` for visited links, `input:focus` for the field being typed in. More specific selectors win over general ones when two rules disagree.
terms.example: `.card:hover { box-shadow: 0 2px 8px gray; }` - a class selector plus a hover state, as the CSS lab asks.

terms.short: The CSS idea that every element is a box made of content, padding, border and margin, from the inside out.
explain: Every element is a rectangle. Its content sits in the middle. Padding is space inside the border, between content and border. The border is the edge line. Margin is space outside the border, pushing other elements away.

By default `width` sets only the content width, so padding and border make the box wider than you asked. `box-sizing: border-box` makes `width` include padding and border, which is easier to reason about and used almost everywhere.
terms.example: A 200px-wide box with 20px padding and a 2px border is 244px wide by default, but exactly 200px with `box-sizing: border-box`.
terms.analogy: A framed picture on a wall: the picture, the mat around it (padding), the frame (border), and the gap to the next frame (margin).

terms.short: JavaScript with types added: you declare what kind of value each variable holds, and mistakes are caught before the code runs.
explain: TypeScript is made by Microsoft. You write `products: Product[] = []` or `function total(price: number): number`, and the compiler checks every use. Passing text where a number is expected is an error at build time, not a surprise in the browser.
It compiles to plain JavaScript, so it runs anywhere JavaScript does. Angular and Ionic projects are written in TypeScript (`.ts` files). In these labs your TypeScript is read rather than run.
terms.example: In the Ionic service lab, `getProducts()` in `api.service.ts` returns `this.http.get(...)` - TypeScript code that compiles to JavaScript.

terms.short: A function you attach to an element that runs whenever a certain event happens, such as a click or a key press.
explain: Browsers fire events all the time: `click`, `input`, `submit`, `keydown`, `load`. `button.addEventListener("click", () => { ... })` says: when this button is clicked, run this function.

The function receives an event object with details, such as which key was pressed. `event.preventDefault()` stops the browser's default action - for a form, the full page reload - so your code can handle it instead.
terms.example: In the DOM lab you add a button and `addEventListener("click", ...)` so each click adds an item to a list.

terms.short: A set of rules that lets one program ask another program to do something.
explain: Programs do not click buttons. When one program needs something from another - the weather, a payment, a list of files - it sends a request in a format both sides agreed on. That agreed format is the API.

Most APIs today work over the web: the request is an HTTP message to a URL called an endpoint, and the answer comes back as JSON. The API hides how the other program works inside; you only need to know what to ask.
terms.example: In the Flask API lab, `GET /api/products` is an endpoint that returns the product rows as JSON, and `POST` to the same path creates a new one.
terms.analogy: A waiter in a restaurant: you never enter the kitchen, you give your order in a fixed format, and the waiter brings back the dish.
terms.why: Portals, command-line tools and scripts in these labs all call the same APIs underneath.

terms.short: A computer, or a program on it, that waits for requests from other computers and answers them.
explain: The word server means a role, not a special kind of hardware. Any computer that runs a program which listens for requests and sends back answers is acting as a server.

A web server returns web pages, a database server returns data, a DNS server returns addresses. Servers usually run all day in a data centre, have no screen, and are managed remotely over the network.
terms.example: When you run `python manage.py runserver` in the Django lab, your project starts a small web server; the Browser tool is the client that asks it for pages.
terms.analogy: A shop assistant behind a counter: they stay in one place, wait for customers, and hand over what is asked for.
terms.why: Most labs build, configure or call a server. When something does not answer, the first question is whether the server is running.

terms.short: The internet's phone book: it turns a name like example.com into the IP address computers need.
explain: People remember names; computers need numbers. The Domain Name System (DNS) is a worldwide set of servers that answer one question: what is the IP address for this name?

Your computer asks a DNS resolver. If the resolver does not know, it asks the servers responsible for that domain, then caches the answer for a while. If DNS is broken, you can still reach a machine by its IP address but not by its name.
terms.example: In the networking lab a host can ping `192.168.10.20` but not `server.lab` until you add a DNS server with a record for that name.
terms.analogy: Looking up a friend's name in your phone's contacts to get the number you actually dial.

terms.short: The part of a URL after the ?, carrying name=value pairs to the server, like ?name=ali&page=2.
explain: `/books/?name=ali&page=2` sends two values: `name` is `ali` and `page` is `2`. Pairs are joined with `&`, and spaces and special characters are encoded (`%20`). A GET form puts its fields here automatically.

The server reads them in its view: Django uses `request.GET.get("name")`, Flask `request.args.get("name")`. Query strings suit searches and filters; never put passwords in them, because URLs are logged and shared.
terms.example: In CS471 Lab 3 a view reads `?name=` from the query string and shows a greeting with it.

terms.short: Scrambling data with a secret key so that only someone with the right key can read it.
explain: Encryption turns readable data (plaintext) into unreadable data (ciphertext) using a key. Only the right key turns it back. It protects data travelling over a network (HTTPS) and data stored on disks.

Symmetric encryption uses one shared key for both directions. Asymmetric encryption uses a pair: a public key anyone may use to encrypt or verify, and a private key kept secret. SSH keys and HTTPS certificates use key pairs.
terms.example: An SSH key pair from `ssh-keygen`: you give GitHub the public key and keep the private key, which must stay readable only by you (`chmod 600`).
terms.analogy: A locked box: anyone can carry it, but only the person with the key can open it.

terms.short: A number from 0 to 65535 that says which program on a computer should receive a piece of network traffic.
explain: One computer runs many network programs at once. The IP address gets data to the right computer; the port number gets it to the right program on that computer.

Well-known services use fixed ports: 80 for HTTP, 443 for HTTPS, 22 for SSH, 53 for DNS, 5432 for PostgreSQL. A program that waits for connections is said to listen on a port. Development servers often use 3000, 5000 or 8000.
terms.example: `http://localhost:5000` means: this same computer, port 5000 - which is where the Flask development server listens in the Flask labs.
terms.analogy: A flat number in an apartment building: the street address finds the building, the flat number finds the right door.

terms.short: A tool that packages an application with everything it needs into an image, and runs it as an isolated container on any machine.
explain: 'It works on my machine' happens because servers differ: another library version, another setting. Docker solves this by packing the app, its libraries and its settings into one image. The image runs the same on a laptop, a test server or the cloud.

A running copy of an image is a container: an isolated process with its own filesystem and network, sharing the host's operating system kernel, so it starts in a second and uses little memory. The Docker daemon (engine) does the work; the `docker` command talks to it.
terms.example: `docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx` downloads the nginx image and runs it as a container called web.
terms.analogy: Shipping containers: whatever is inside, every crane and ship handles the box the same way.
terms.why: The Docker and data infrastructure labs build images and run containers on a simulated Docker engine.

terms.short: A text file of instructions - start FROM this base, COPY these files, RUN this command - that Docker follows to build an image.
explain: Each line is an instruction: `FROM python:3.12-slim` picks the base image, `WORKDIR /app` sets the folder, `COPY requirements.txt .` copies files from the build context, `RUN pip install -r requirements.txt` runs a command, `CMD ["python","main.py"]` sets what runs at start.
The build context is the folder sent to the builder; `.dockerignore` keeps secrets and junk out of it. `docker build -t myapp:1.0 .` builds and tags the image.
terms.example: FROM, WORKDIR, COPY requirements, RUN pip install, COPY source, CMD - in that order so dependencies stay cached.

terms.short: Docker reuses already-built image layers when an instruction and its inputs have not changed, so ordering the Dockerfile well makes rebuilds fast.
explain: Every Dockerfile instruction makes a layer. When rebuilding, Docker checks each step: same instruction and same files as last time? Then it reuses the cached layer. The first step that changed, and every step after it, is rebuilt.
So copy what changes rarely first. Copy `requirements.txt` and install dependencies before copying your source; then a code change rebuilds only the last layer instead of reinstalling every package.
terms.example: With source copied before `pip install`, every code edit reinstalls all packages; swapped, the dependency layer stays CACHED.

terms.short: A packaged app with everything it needs, running isolated on a shared operating system - lighter than a virtual machine.
explain: An app needs the right libraries and settings to run. A container image bundles the app with all of them. Starting that image gives a container: an isolated process with its own files and network, but sharing the host's operating system kernel.

Because there is no separate operating system to boot, a container starts in a second and uses little memory. The same image runs the same way on a laptop and on a server. Docker made containers popular; Kubernetes runs many of them.
terms.example: `docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx` starts a web server container from the `nginx` image and connects host port 8080 to it.
terms.analogy: A shipping container: whatever is inside, it is loaded, moved and stacked the same way on any ship or truck.

terms.short: The | symbol in a shell, which sends the output of one command straight into the next command as its input.
explain: Linux tools are small and each does one job: `grep` keeps matching lines, `sort` sorts, `uniq` removes repeats, `wc -l` counts lines. A pipe `|` connects them, so the text flows from one to the next without temporary files.

`cut -d' ' -f1 access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr` reads like a sentence: take the first field, sort it, count each value, sort by count, biggest first. Order matters - `uniq` only removes repeats that are next to each other, so `sort` must come first.
terms.example: `grep 404 access.log | wc -l` counts how many lines of the log mention 404 - a task in the text-processing lab.
terms.analogy: A factory line where each worker does one small job and passes the piece to the next.

track.tagline: Models, migrations, views and templates on a database that really exists.
what: Django is a popular Python web framework for database-backed websites; Instagram and many others use it. It comes with an ORM, migrations, templates, forms and an automatic admin, so you can build a working site quickly.

In this track you build a small product site against a real database: you write models, run `makemigrations` and `migrate`, query with the ORM and watch the SQL, then open the page your view returned.
how: A request arrives, `urls.py` matches its path and calls a view. The view uses models - Python classes mapped to tables - through the ORM to read or write rows, then renders a template with the data and returns HTML or JSON.

Changing a model means a migration: `makemigrations` writes it, `migrate` applies it. Forms post back to views and are protected by a CSRF token. The admin site gives a ready-made back office once you register your models.
track.who: Python developers building websites or APIs, and back-end developers learning a full framework.
learn: Explain what settings.py, urls.py and views.py each do
Turn a model class into a table with makemigrations and migrate
Create, read, update and delete with the ORM and read the SQL it runs
Route URLs with parameters to views returning HTML or JSON
Build layouts with template inheritance, loops and filters
Handle forms with POST, CSRF and Post/Redirect/Get
Model a ForeignKey relation and spot an N+1 query
Register models in the admin and create a superuser
before: Basic Python, including classes: see the Python track.
Basic SQL helps to read the generated queries: see the SQL track's first labs.
Read the glossary entries for HTTP and URL.
track.simulated: The `manage.py` commands are simulated over a real SQLite database: migrations run real CREATE TABLE statements and the ORM issues real SQL, while your views and templates are read rather than executed.

terms.short: The set of rules browsers and servers use to ask for and send web pages and data.
explain: HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is a conversation of requests and responses. A request has a method (GET to read, POST to send data, PUT/PATCH to change, DELETE to remove), a path such as `/books/`, and headers.
