The response starts with a status code: 200 means OK, 201 created, 301/302 moved, 404 not found, 405 method not allowed, 500 the server failed. Then come headers and the body - an HTML page, an image or JSON.
terms.example: In the Wireshark lab you open a `GET / HTTP/1.1` request and the `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` response that answered it, header by header.
terms.analogy: Ordering at a counter with a fixed form: tick what you want (method), write the item (path), and the reply comes back stamped OK or Not found.
terms.why: Every web, API and backend lab sends HTTP. Reading the method and status code is the fastest way to find what went wrong.

terms.short: The full address of something on the web, such as https://example.com/books/12/?name=ali.
explain: A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) has parts. The scheme (`https://`) says how to talk. The host (`example.com`) says which server. An optional port follows a colon. The path (`/books/12/`) says what you want on that server.

After a `?` comes the query string, `name=ali`, extra values for the server. After a `#` comes a fragment, used only by the browser. Web frameworks such as Django and Flask read the path to decide which code runs.
terms.example: In the Django labs `/books/index2/12/` routes to a view that receives `12` as a parameter, and `/books/?name=ali` passes `ali` in the query string.
terms.analogy: A full postal address: country, city, street, house, and a note for the person who opens the door.

terms.short: A popular Python web framework that gives you everything to build a database-backed website: URLs, views, templates, models and an admin.
explain: Django was released in 2005 and powers sites such as Instagram. A framework decides the structure for you: URL patterns send each request to a view function, the view uses models to read the database, and a template turns the data into HTML.
It is 'batteries included': an ORM, migrations, forms with CSRF protection, user authentication and an automatic admin site come built in. You drive it from the command line with `python manage.py`.
terms.example: The Django labs build a product site: `startproject`, a `Product` model, `makemigrations` and `migrate`, views, templates and the admin.
terms.why: Both the Django track and the CS471 course labs build Django projects step by step.

terms.short: A Python class that describes one database table: each attribute is a column with a type.
explain: In Django, `class Product(models.Model): name = models.CharField(max_length=100); price = models.DecimalField(max_digits=8, decimal_places=2)` describes a `products` table. Each instance of the class is one row. An `id` primary key is added automatically.

Field types decide the column type and validation; options such as `default`, `null` and `unique` add rules. Flask's SQLAlchemy models (`class Product(db.Model)`) are the same idea. Changing a model needs a migration to change the table.
terms.example: In the Django models lab you define `Product` with `price` as a `DecimalField`, then run `makemigrations` and `migrate` so the table really exists.

terms.short: A small script that changes a database's structure step by step - creating a table, adding a column - to match your models.
explain: You change a model in Python; the real table must change too. In Django `python manage.py makemigrations` compares models with the last migration and writes a new migration file. `python manage.py migrate` runs it against the database (CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE).

Migrations are numbered and committed to Git, so every developer and server applies the same changes in the same order. `sqlmigrate` shows the SQL a migration will run. Flask uses Alembic: `flask db migrate` then `flask db upgrade`.
terms.example: `makemigrations` writes `0001_initial.py`, `sqlmigrate shop 0001` prints its `CREATE TABLE`, and `migrate` actually creates the table.
terms.why: A missing `migrate` is the most common reason a Django or Flask lab says 'no such table'.

terms.short: Object-Relational Mapper: a library that lets you read and write database rows as Python objects instead of writing SQL.
explain: With an ORM, `Product.objects.filter(price__lt=20)` (Django) or `Product.query.filter(Product.price < 20)` (SQLAlchemy) becomes `SELECT ... FROM products WHERE price < 20`, and each row comes back as a `Product` object.
You still need to know what SQL it produces: one innocent-looking loop can fire hundreds of queries. The labs show the SQL every ORM call runs, so you can see the translation.
terms.example: In the ORM lab, `Product.objects.create(name="Mug", price=8.5)` issues an INSERT, and the query log shows the exact SQL.

terms.short: The function in a web framework that receives a request and returns the response - a page, JSON or a redirect.
explain: A view is ordinary Python: `def product_list(request): products = Product.objects.all(); return render(request, "list.html", {"products": products})`. It reads input (URL parameters, query string, form data), talks to models, and builds a response.

Django offers `HttpResponse` for plain text or HTML, `JsonResponse` for JSON, `render` to fill a template, and `redirect` to send the browser elsewhere. In Flask, the function under an `@app.route` decorator is the view.
terms.example: In the views lab, `def detail(request, pk): p = get_object_or_404(Product, pk=pk)` reads the int parameter from the URL and renders one product.

terms.short: The table that maps each URL path to the view that should handle it, like /products/7/ to product_detail.
explain: In Django, `urls.py` holds `urlpatterns = [path("products/<int:pk>/", views.detail, name="detail")]`. When a request arrives, Django tries each pattern in order; the first match calls its view, passing captured parts such as `pk=7`.

A project's `urls.py` can `include()` each app's URLconf under a prefix such as `/books/`. Naming a pattern lets templates build links with `{% url 'detail' p.id %}` instead of hard-coding paths. No match means 404.
terms.example: In CS471 Lab 3, `/books/index2/12/` matches `<int:val>` and calls the view, while `/books/index2/text/` matches nothing and gives a 404.

terms.short: An HTML file with placeholders and simple logic, which the framework fills with data to produce the final page.
explain: A template mixes HTML with template language: `{{ product.name }}` prints a value, `{% for p in products %} ... {% empty %} ... {% endfor %}` loops, `{% if %}` decides, and filters change values: `{{ price|floatformat:2 }}`.

The view passes a context dictionary and the template engine produces HTML. Values are auto-escaped, so a product named `<script>` is shown as text rather than run. Flask uses Jinja, which looks almost the same.
terms.example:
In the templates lab, a list template loops `{% for p in products %}
  • {{ p.name }}
    • {% endfor %}` and links each with `{% url %}`.

terms.short: Django's automatic back-office website for viewing and editing your models' data, opened by a superuser at /admin/.
explain: Django builds a full management interface from your models. Register a model in the app's `admin.py` with `admin.site.register(Product)` and it gets list, add, edit and delete pages - no HTML needed.

To log in you need a superuser, created with `python manage.py createsuperuser`; it is stored as a row in the `auth_user` table with a hashed password. The auth tables come from Django's own migrations, so `migrate` must run first.
terms.example: In the admin lab: `migrate`, `createsuperuser`, register your models, add a `__str__` so rows show real names, then find your user in the database.

terms.short: The four basic things you do with stored data: Create, Read, Update and Delete.
explain: Almost every data screen is CRUD: a form to add (Create), a list and detail page (Read), an edit form (Update) and a delete button (Delete). In SQL they are INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE; in a REST API, POST, GET, PUT/PATCH and DELETE.
A typical CRUD resource in a web app has routes for list, detail, add, edit and delete. Input must be validated before it reaches the database.
terms.example: The last Flask lab builds a complete CRUD app: at least four routes, an add view that handles GET and POST, and a list template.

terms.short: A popular, easy-to-read programming language used for websites, scripts, data work and AI.
explain: Python programs are plain text files ending in `.py`. The language is known for readable code: blocks are marked by indentation instead of braces, and names read almost like English - `for item in items:`.

Python runs your code line by line through an interpreter, so you can try things quickly. It comes with a large standard library, and thousands of extra libraries add web frameworks (Django, Flask), data tools and AI.
terms.example: `print(f"Total: {price * 2}")` prints a calculated value - the kind of line you write in the first Python lab.
terms.why: The Python, Django, Flask and data labs all run real Python. Reading a traceback is the most useful Python skill.

terms.short: A Django project is the whole website with its settings; an app is one self-contained part of it, such as books or users.
explain: `django-admin startproject libraryproject` creates the project: `manage.py` plus a package holding `settings.py`, the main `urls.py` and `wsgi.py`. `python manage.py startapp bookmodule` creates an app with its own `models.py`, `views.py` and `apps.py`.
An app only takes part once it is listed in `INSTALLED_APPS` in `settings.py` - forget that and its models get no tables. Splitting features into apps keeps a large project organised.
terms.example: In CS471 Lab 2 you create `bookmodule` and `usermodule` inside `apps/`, set their `name` to `'apps.bookmodule'`, and add both to `INSTALLED_APPS`.

terms.short: A named, reusable block of code that takes inputs (parameters), does a job and can give back a result.
explain: `def total(price, qty=1): return price * qty` defines a function called `total`. `price` and `qty` are parameters; `qty=1` is a default used when the caller leaves it out. `return` sends the result back. Calling `total(8.5, qty=3)` runs it.

Functions let you write a piece of logic once and use it everywhere. `*args` collects extra positional arguments, `**kwargs` extra named ones. Never use a list as a default (`items=[]`) - it is shared between calls; use `None` instead.
terms.example: In the functions lab, `def safe(items=None): items = items or []` is the safe form of a mutable default.
terms.analogy: A vending machine: put in the inputs, press the button, and the same job is done every time.

terms.short: The program inside a terminal that reads each command you type, runs it, and shows the result.
explain: The shell (on Linux usually `bash`) waits at a prompt. You type a line; it splits the line into a program name and arguments, finds that program, runs it, and prints what it outputs. Then it waits again.

The shell also adds powerful features: `|` pipes one command's output into another, `>` saves output to a file, `*` matches many file names, and `$NAME` uses a variable. A file of shell commands is a shell script.
terms.example: In `cat access.log | grep 404 | wc -l` the shell starts three programs and connects them, then prints the final count.
terms.analogy: An interpreter between you and the operating system: you speak in short commands, it passes them on and reports back.

terms.short: Proving who you are to a system, for example with a password, a key or a code from your phone.
explain: Before a system lets you do anything it asks: who are you? You answer with something you know (a password), something you have (a phone, an SSH key, a token) or something you are (a fingerprint). Using two of these is two-factor authentication.
Authentication only answers who. What you are then allowed to do is a separate question, called authorization. Programs authenticate too, usually with API keys or tokens instead of passwords.
terms.example: In the Django admin lab, `createsuperuser` stores a username and a hashed password; logging in to `/admin/` checks the password against that hash.
terms.analogy: Showing your ID card at the entrance of a building.

terms.short: An organised store of data that a program can search, add to and change quickly and safely.
explain: A database keeps data in a structured way so it can find any item fast, even among millions. Most databases store tables of rows and columns and are asked questions in SQL; others store documents or key-value pairs.

The database program also protects the data: two users changing the same row at once do not corrupt it, a half-finished change can be undone, and nothing is lost if the program stops. SQLite, PostgreSQL and MySQL are common examples.
terms.example: The SQL labs query a real SQLite database of 275,000 rows; the Django and Flask labs create their own tables in one with `migrate`.
terms.analogy: A library with a catalogue: books are stored in order and a librarian finds any one in seconds.

terms.short: A command-line tool that sends an HTTP request and prints the response - the quickest way to test an API.
explain: `curl http://localhost:5000/api/products` sends a GET and prints the body. `-i` also shows the status line and headers. `-X POST` changes the method, `-H "Content-Type: application/json"` adds a header, and `-d '{"name":"Mug"}'` sends a body.
Because curl has no browser around it, it shows exactly what the server returns - useful for debugging an API from the outside in before blaming the frontend.
terms.example: `curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"name":"Mug","price":8.5}' localhost:5000/api/products` creates a product in the Flask API lab.

terms.short: A small web server built into a framework for testing on your own machine, started with a command like runserver.
explain: `python manage.py runserver` (Django), `flask run` (Flask) or `ionic serve` (Ionic) start a server on your computer, usually at `http://127.0.0.1:8000`, `5000` or `8100`. Open that address in a browser to see your site.

It reloads when you change code and prints every request with its status code in the terminal - useful for debugging. It is not built for real traffic or security; production uses a proper server such as Gunicorn behind Nginx.
terms.example: In the first Django lab you start the development server and the site root answers 200 in the Browser tool.

terms.short: A Linux command that prints only the lines of text that contain a word or pattern.
explain: `grep pattern file` reads the file line by line and prints each line that matches. Useful flags: `-i` ignores case, `-v` keeps lines that do NOT match, `-c` counts matches, `-n` shows line numbers, and `-r` searches every file in a directory tree.
The pattern can be a regular expression, a small language for text patterns, such as `^ERROR` (lines starting with ERROR). `grep` searches inside files; to find files by their name, use `find`.
terms.example: `grep -r "TODO" .` searches inside every file under the current directory for the word TODO.

terms.short: A free, open-source operating system that runs most of the world's servers, phones (Android) and cloud machines.
explain: Linux was started in 1991 by Linus Torvalds and is developed by thousands of people. Strictly, Linux is the kernel - the core that talks to the hardware - and a distribution such as Ubuntu adds the shell, tools and package manager around it.
On servers Linux is used mostly through a terminal, not a desktop. Everything is a file in one tree starting at `/`, programs are small tools that each do one job, and you combine them in the shell.
terms.example: The Linux labs give you a real shell in your own directory: `ls`, `cd`, `grep`, `chmod`, `tar` and pipes all behave as on a real Linux server.
terms.why: Docker, Kubernetes, the cloud and most servers run Linux, so these commands appear in almost every later lab.

terms.short: A text window where you type commands to a computer and read what it prints back.
explain: A terminal is the window; it shows text and sends your keystrokes. Inside it runs a shell, the program that reads your command, runs it, and shows the output. People often say terminal, console and command line for the same thing.

In these labs the terminal is a tool beside the others, working on the same files. You type a command after the prompt (such as `student@lab:~$`) and press Enter. Up arrow repeats an earlier command; Tab completes names.
terms.example: Open the Linux Terminal, type `pwd` and press Enter: the shell prints the directory you are in.
terms.analogy: A chat window with the computer: you write a message (a command) and it writes back.

terms.short: HTTP sent through an encrypted connection, so nobody in between can read or change it.
explain: Plain HTTP travels as readable text: anyone on the same Wi-Fi or along the route could see passwords or change the page. HTTPS wraps the same HTTP messages in TLS encryption.

When the connection starts, the server shows a certificate proving its name, and both sides agree on secret keys. After that every byte is encrypted. The browser shows a padlock. HTTPS normally uses port 443.
terms.example: The Wireshark lab browses `neverssl.com` precisely because it uses plain HTTP; on an HTTPS site the capture would show only encrypted bytes.
terms.analogy: Sending a letter in a locked box that only the receiver can open, instead of on a postcard anyone can read.

terms.short: A set of rules that lets one program ask another program to do something.
explain: Programs do not click buttons. When one program needs something from another - the weather, a payment, a list of files - it sends a request in a format both sides agreed on. That agreed format is the API.

Most APIs today work over the web: the request is an HTTP message to a URL called an endpoint, and the answer comes back as JSON. The API hides how the other program works inside; you only need to know what to ask.
terms.example: In the Flask API lab, `GET /api/products` is an endpoint that returns the product rows as JSON, and `POST` to the same path creates a new one.
terms.analogy: A waiter in a restaurant: you never enter the kitchen, you give your order in a fixed format, and the waiter brings back the dish.
terms.why: Portals, command-line tools and scripts in these labs all call the same APIs underneath.

terms.short: A computer, or a program on it, that waits for requests from other computers and answers them.
explain: The word server means a role, not a special kind of hardware. Any computer that runs a program which listens for requests and sends back answers is acting as a server.

A web server returns web pages, a database server returns data, a DNS server returns addresses. Servers usually run all day in a data centre, have no screen, and are managed remotely over the network.
terms.example: When you run `python manage.py runserver` in the Django lab, your project starts a small web server; the Browser tool is the client that asks it for pages.
terms.analogy: A shop assistant behind a counter: they stay in one place, wait for customers, and hand over what is asked for.
terms.why: Most labs build, configure or call a server. When something does not answer, the first question is whether the server is running.

terms.short: A program that sends a request to a server and uses the answer it gets back.
explain: A client starts the conversation. Your web browser is a client: you type an address, it sends a request to a web server, and it shows the page that comes back.
Clients are not only browsers. The `git` command talking to GitHub, `curl` calling an API, and a phone app loading a list are all clients. One server usually serves many clients at the same time.
terms.example: In the Ionic full-stack lab the phone app is the client: it calls the Flask API (the server) and shows the rows it gets back.
terms.analogy: A customer in a restaurant: you ask for something, then wait for it to be brought to you.

terms.short: The internet's phone book: it turns a name like example.com into the IP address computers need.
explain: People remember names; computers need numbers. The Domain Name System (DNS) is a worldwide set of servers that answer one question: what is the IP address for this name?

Your computer asks a DNS resolver. If the resolver does not know, it asks the servers responsible for that domain, then caches the answer for a while. If DNS is broken, you can still reach a machine by its IP address but not by its name.
terms.example: In the networking lab a host can ping `192.168.10.20` but not `server.lab` until you add a DNS server with a record for that name.
terms.analogy: Looking up a friend's name in your phone's contacts to get the number you actually dial.

terms.short: The part of a URL after the ?, carrying name=value pairs to the server, like ?name=ali&page=2.
explain: `/books/?name=ali&page=2` sends two values: `name` is `ali` and `page` is `2`. Pairs are joined with `&`, and spaces and special characters are encoded (`%20`). A GET form puts its fields here automatically.

The server reads them in its view: Django uses `request.GET.get("name")`, Flask `request.args.get("name")`. Query strings suit searches and filters; never put passwords in them, because URLs are logged and shared.
terms.example: In CS471 Lab 3 a view reads `?name=` from the query string and shows a greeting with it.

terms.short: Data arranged in rows and columns: each row is one record, each column one property, such as name or price.
explain: A database table looks like a spreadsheet sheet with strict rules. Every column has a name and a type (whole number, text, date). Every row is one thing: one customer, one order, one product.

A primary key column, usually `id`, gives each row a unique identifier, and other tables point to it. You read a table with `SELECT`, and you define it with `CREATE TABLE` - or, in Django and Flask, by writing a model class.
terms.example: The `orders` table in the SQL labs has a row per order and columns such as `order_id`, `customer_id`, `country` and `amount`.
terms.analogy: A class register: each line is a student, each column a detail like name or grade.

terms.short: A class is a blueprint for objects; an object is one thing made from it, with its own data (attributes) and actions (methods).
explain: `class Account:` defines a blueprint. `__init__(self, owner)` runs when an object is created and stores attributes on `self`, such as `self.balance = 0`. Methods are functions inside the class: `def deposit(self, amount):`.

`acc = Account("Ali")` creates an object (an instance). A subclass, `class Savings(Account):`, inherits everything and adds or changes behaviour; `super().__init__(owner)` calls the parent. Django and SQLAlchemy models are classes.
terms.example: In the classes lab: an `Account` with a `deposit` method that changes `self.balance`, a `__str__` so `print(acc)` reads well, and a `Savings` subclass.
terms.analogy: A cookie cutter is the class; each cookie is an object - same shape, but each can have its own icing.

terms.short: The planned structure of data: which tables or fields exist, their names, their types and how they connect.
explain: Before storing data, you decide its shape: a `products` table with `id` (integer), `name` (text) and `price` (decimal). That plan is the schema. The database uses it to reject data that does not fit, such as text in a number column.
Changing a schema later - adding a column, renaming a table - must be done carefully, because existing data and code depend on it. Django and Flask use migrations to apply such changes step by step.
terms.example: `.schema products` in SQLite prints the `CREATE TABLE` statement that defines the table's columns - its schema.
terms.analogy: The blueprint of a building: it decides the rooms before anyone moves in.

terms.short: The migration tool for SQLAlchemy; with Flask-Migrate you run flask db init, migrate and upgrade.
explain: Three commands make the cycle. `flask db init` once, to set up the `migrations/` folder. `flask db migrate -m "add product"` compares your models with the database and writes a revision file. `flask db upgrade` runs it, creating or altering tables.
`db.create_all()` is not a migration: it creates missing tables but never changes existing ones and keeps no history, so a later model change is silently not applied. Real projects use migrations.
terms.example: In the Flask database lab: set up Alembic, generate a revision, apply it, then find the table from SQL.

terms.short: Django's object for a database query that has not run yet; you chain filters onto it and it runs when you use the results.
explain: `Product.objects.all()` returns a QuerySet. Each method returns a new one: `.filter(price__lt=20)`, `.exclude(stock=0)`, `.order_by("-price")`, `[:5]` for a limit. Nothing hits the database until you loop, print or count it.

Field lookups use double underscores: `title__icontains="and"`, `price__lte=80`. `.get(id=1)` returns exactly one object and raises an error if there are zero or several; `.filter()` returns any number, possibly none.
terms.example: In CS471 Lab 7, `Book.objects.filter(title__icontains="and").exclude(edition=1)[:5]` chains filter, exclude and slicing.

terms.short: The most widely used Python ORM; Flask uses it through Flask-SQLAlchemy to map classes to tables.
explain: You declare `class Product(db.Model): id = db.Column(db.Integer, primary_key=True); name = db.Column(db.String(80), nullable=False)`. SQLAlchemy turns that into a table and each object into a row.

Queries read like Python: `Product.query.filter_by(name="Mug").first()` (equality only), `Product.query.filter(Product.price > 20).all()` (any expression), `.order_by(Product.price.desc())`. Writes go through the session and are saved by `commit()`. Columns are nullable unless you say otherwise - the opposite of Django.
terms.example: In the Flask database lab you declare a `Product` model with a primary key, then generate and apply a migration to create its table.

terms.short: The language used to ask a database questions and change its data, e.g. SELECT name FROM customers.
explain: SQL (Structured Query Language) is written as short statements that read almost like English. `SELECT` reads rows, `INSERT` adds, `UPDATE` changes, `DELETE` removes, and `CREATE TABLE` defines a new table.

You say what you want, not how to find it: `SELECT name FROM customers WHERE country = 'Jordan'` - and the database decides the fastest way. Almost every database speaks SQL, with small differences between products.
terms.example: `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE country = 'Jordan';` counts the orders from Jordan - one of the first tasks in the SQL labs.
terms.analogy: Asking a librarian a precise question - 'all books by this author after 2010' - instead of searching the shelves yourself.
terms.why: SQL appears in the SQL, Django, Flask and every data lab. The ORMs in Django and Flask write SQL for you, and the labs show it.

terms.short: In Flask, the @app.route line above a function that says which URL path, and which HTTP methods, that function answers.
explain: `@app.route("/products/<int:pid>")` before `def detail(pid):` connects the path to the function; Flask passes the captured `pid` as an argument. The `@` line is a decorator: it registers the function without changing it.
By default a route accepts only GET. `@app.route("/add", methods=["GET", "POST"])` accepts both, and inside you test `request.method`. A POST to a GET-only route gets `405 Method Not Allowed`.
terms.example: In the first Flask lab you write a route at `/`, one that takes a parameter, and one that accepts POST - then see a 405 when the method is wrong.

terms.short: Writing one base layout with named blocks, which every page extends and fills in, so shared parts are written once.
explain: `base.html` holds the parts every page shares - `<head>`, navigation, footer - and leaves holes: `{% block content %}{% endblock %}`. A page starts with `{% extends "base.html" %}` and fills `{% block content %}`.
Change the navigation once in the base and every page updates. `{% include "nav.html" %}` inserts a reusable fragment. Django and Flask's Jinja both work this way.
terms.example: In CS471 Lab 4 you create `base.html` with blocks and includes, then make the three pages extend it.
terms.analogy: Printed letterhead paper: the logo and footer are already there, you only write the middle.

terms.short: The template language used by Flask (and Ansible): HTML with {{ values }} and {% tags %} for loops and conditions.
explain: `render_template("list.html", products=rows)` fills a Jinja template. `{{ p.name }}` prints, `{% for p in products %}...{% endfor %}` loops, `{% extends "base.html" %}` and `{% block %}` give a shared layout.

It looks like Django's templates with small differences: Jinja allows real Python-like expressions and function calls (`{{ items|length }}`, `{{ loop.index }}`), and uses `{% else %}` on a for loop where Django uses `{% empty %}`.
terms.example: In the Flask templates lab, a page extends `base.html` and loops over a list passed in from the view.

track.tagline: One place for a company's data: ingestion, lakehouses, Delta, a SQL warehouse, semantic models, governance and CI/CD.
what: Microsoft Fabric is Microsoft's all-in-one data platform. It combines what used to be separate products - data pipelines, Spark, a data warehouse and Power BI reports - in one web product, with all data stored once in OneLake.

This track builds a Service Operations data product: ServiceNow tickets are ingested, cleaned through bronze, silver and gold layers, modelled for reporting, secured, quality-gated, governed and released through CI/CD.
how: A company buys capacity; teams get workspaces on it; inside a workspace they create items - lakehouses, warehouses, notebooks, pipelines, semantic models. Every table is a Delta table in OneLake, so the warehouse, notebooks and reports read the same copy.

Pipelines copy data in, notebooks transform it with PySpark, the warehouse serves T-SQL, and semantic models with DAX measures feed Power BI through Direct Lake. Git integration and deployment pipelines move work from dev to production.
track.who: Data engineers, analytics engineers and BI developers in companies that use Microsoft 365 or Azure, and people preparing for the Fabric data engineer certification.
learn: Plan capacity, workspaces, roles and OneLake
Ingest the ServiceNow Table API incrementally and resiliently
Build medallion layers with PySpark, MERGE and Delta maintenance
Model gold tables and a Direct Lake semantic model with DAX
Secure data with item permissions, RLS and labels, and handle GDPR
Release with Git, PR checks and deployment pipelines
Monitor runs and fix capacity and Spark performance
before: What a table, a file and a database are
track.simulated: The Fabric tenant is simulated: workspaces, items, Delta tables, pipelines and models follow Fabric's real rules and refusals on sample ServiceNow data, but no Microsoft service is called.

terms.short: Microsoft's all-in-one data platform: storage, data pipelines, Spark notebooks, a SQL warehouse and Power BI reports in one product.
explain: A company's data usually passes through many tools: one to copy it in, one to store it, one to transform it, one to report on it. Microsoft Fabric puts those in one web product, sold as capacity that a whole organisation shares.

Everything lives in workspaces and is stored once in OneLake, a single data lake for the whole company. Inside a workspace you create items: lakehouses, warehouses, notebooks, pipelines, semantic models and reports.
It is driven from the Fabric portal in a browser, from its REST API, or from the `fab` command line.
terms.example: `fab mkdir ws-ops-dev.Workspace -P capacityName=cap-ops-f8` creates a development workspace on a capacity.
terms.why: The Fabric Data Engineering track builds a Service Operations data product end to end in a simulated Fabric tenant.

terms.short: The pool of computing power a company buys for Fabric, measured in capacity units (CU); every workspace on it shares that power.
explain: Fabric is paid for as a capacity with a size like F8 or F64 - the number is how many capacity units (CU) it provides. A workspace must be assigned to a capacity before it can hold items.

Usage is smoothed over time, so a short spike borrows from the future. Sustained overuse leads to throttling: first interactive work is delayed, then rejected. One noisy item can starve everyone - the fix is usually the workload, not a bigger SKU. Surge protection limits background jobs.
terms.example: The capacity lab finds the notebook burning most CU in the metrics view and fixes it instead of scaling up.

terms.short: A shared folder in a data or analytics product (Fabric, Log Analytics) that holds a team's items and controls who can use them through roles.
explain: In Fabric a workspace holds items - lakehouses, notebooks, pipelines, reports - for one team or one environment. Separate workspaces for development and production keep experiments away from what users rely on.

Access is given with workspace roles: Admin, Member, Contributor, Viewer. Give roles to groups, not individual people, and give the smallest role that works. A workspace identity lets pipelines sign in without anyone's personal password.
terms.example: The platform lab creates `ws-ops-dev` and `ws-ops-prod` and gives the analysts group Viewer on production only.

terms.short: Fabric's single data lake for the whole organisation: every lakehouse and warehouse stores its tables there, as Delta files.
explain: Instead of each team keeping its own storage account, Fabric gives every tenant one OneLake, like OneDrive for data. Each workspace and item is a folder in it, and tables are stored in the open Delta format.

Because there is only one copy, a warehouse, a notebook and a report can all read the same table without copying it. Shortcuts point at data in other places without moving it, and OneLake data access roles restrict folders.
terms.example: A table written by a notebook into `lh_silver` is immediately readable by the warehouse with a three-part name.

terms.short: A Fabric item that stores both files and tables in OneLake, worked on with Spark, with a read-only SQL endpoint for queries.
explain: A lakehouse combines a data lake (any files, cheap storage) with database-like tables. It has a Files area for raw data and a Tables area of Delta tables.

Notebooks write to it with Spark. Every lakehouse also gets a SQL analytics endpoint for T-SQL queries, but that endpoint is read-only - writes in SQL need a warehouse. Teams often create three: bronze, silver and gold.
terms.example: `fab mkdir ws-ops-dev.Workspace/lh_bronze.Lakehouse` creates the bronze lakehouse.

terms.short: Organising a data lake in three quality layers: bronze is raw data as received, silver is cleaned, gold is shaped for reports.
explain: Data arrives messy. Bronze keeps it exactly as it came, append-only, with lineage columns (when, from where) so you can always reprocess. Silver deduplicates, fixes types and quarantines bad rows - one clean row per business record.
Gold reshapes silver for consumers: facts and dimensions, aggregates, data products. Each layer is its own lakehouse or folder, so permissions and quality checks can differ per layer.
terms.example: ServiceNow incidents land in `lh_bronze`, are deduplicated into `lh_silver`, and modelled into `fact_incident` in gold.

terms.short: A table stored as Parquet files plus a transaction log, giving a data lake database features: safe updates, MERGE, history and undo.
explain: Plain files cannot be updated safely - two writers clash and a failed write leaves half a table. Delta Lake adds a log of every change (commit). Readers see a consistent version, MERGE can upsert, and every old version is kept for a while.

`DESCRIBE HISTORY` lists versions, time travel reads an old one and RESTORE rolls back a bad write. OPTIMIZE compacts many small files; VACUUM deletes files no version needs any more - with a retention period that protects readers. Schema changes must be made deliberately.
terms.example: After a bad overwrite, `RESTORE TABLE silver.incident TO VERSION AS OF 12` brings the old data back.

terms.short: A Fabric item that moves and orchestrates data with activities such as Copy, Lookup and ForEach, run on a schedule or on demand.
explain: A pipeline is a flow of activities. Copy moves data from a source (the ServiceNow API, a database) to a destination (a lakehouse). Lookup reads a value, ForEach repeats steps for each item, Notebook runs code.

Activities have retry policies for temporary errors like API throttling. A metadata-driven pipeline reads a control table listing the sources, so a new source is one new row, not a new pipeline. A failed run can be rerun from the failed activity.
terms.example: One pipeline: Lookup the control table, ForEach source, Copy from the Table API since the last watermark.

terms.short: A Fabric item that is a full SQL data warehouse: you create, load and query tables with T-SQL, and it stores them in OneLake.
explain: Where a lakehouse is driven by Spark, a warehouse is driven by T-SQL, Microsoft's SQL dialect: `CREATE TABLE`, `INSERT`, stored procedures, views. It supports multi-table transactions.

CTAS (`CREATE TABLE AS SELECT`) builds a table from a query in one step. Three-part names (`lh_silver.dbo.incident`) query another item in the workspace. It refuses some data types, so tables are created with warehouse-supported types.
terms.example: `CREATE TABLE dbo.daily_incidents AS SELECT ... FROM lh_silver.dbo.incident GROUP BY ...`

terms.short: A business-friendly layer over data tables - relationships, measures and names - that Power BI reports and analysts query.
explain: Raw tables are not what a manager wants to see. A semantic model defines which tables relate to which (an incident to its date and its group), and measures written in DAX such as 'SLA met %'. Reports query the model, so every report uses the same definitions.
A date table is marked as the calendar, relationships are usually single-direction from dimensions to facts, and row-level security can limit which rows each person sees.
terms.example: The model relates `fact_incident` to `dim_date` and `dim_group`, and defines `Incidents`, `MTTR hours` and `SLA met %`.

terms.short: A web-based system companies use as their IT help desk and operations hub: every incident, request, problem and change is a ticket in it.
explain: When something breaks in a company - the website is down, a laptop will not start - someone has to record it, decide how urgent it is, assign it to a team and track it until it is fixed. ServiceNow is the most widely used product for that, made by the company of the same name.

It stores tickets in tables: `incident`, `problem`, `change_request`, plus the CMDB (the list of every server and application). Each ticket has a priority, an assigned group, timers for its service-level agreement, and a history of comments.
Monitoring tools create tickets in it automatically, and data teams pull its tables into reports through its Table API.
terms.example: In the SLA lab you acknowledge P1 incident `INC0010021` in the ServiceNow queue within its 15-minute pick-up target.
terms.analogy: The front desk and logbook of a hospital for computers: every patient (problem) is registered, triaged, assigned a doctor and tracked until discharged.
terms.why: The Cloud Operations labs run a 24/7 support contract through a simulated ServiceNow, and the Fabric labs ingest its tables.

terms.short: The configuration management database: ServiceNow's list of every server, application and service, and how they depend on each other.
explain: Each thing IT manages - a server, a database, an application, a business service - is a configuration item (CI) in the CMDB, with relationships such as 'runs on' and 'depends on'.

With good data you can answer 'if this server fails, which services are hit?'. Bad data - duplicate CIs, relationships pointing at deleted CIs, dependency cycles - makes impact maps wrong. CSDM is ServiceNow's standard model for layering business services over technical ones.
terms.example: The CMDB lab maps duplicate CIs to a survivor, removes orphaned relationships and builds a service-impact map.

terms.short: A service-level agreement: a promise, often in a contract, of how fast a ticket will be picked up, answered and resolved, measured by timers.
explain: An SLA turns 'we will be quick' into numbers. A 24/7 contract might say a P1 must be picked up in 15 minutes, the customer answered in 30, and service restored in 2 hours.

Each target is a clock that starts with the ticket and stops at a defined event - acknowledgement, the first customer-visible comment, resolution. Some clocks pause while a ticket waits on the customer, but a 24/7 P1 cannot be put on hold. A missed SLA can cost money.
terms.example: P1: pick-up SLA stops when you acknowledge, response SLA when you post a customer comment, restore SLA when you resolve.

terms.short: A dataset treated as a product: it has an owner, documentation, a contract, an SLA and consumers, rather than being a by-product of a pipeline.
explain: A table that 'just exists' has no one to ask when it breaks. A data product has an accountable team, a clear purpose, a published contract, quality checks, an SLA and a catalogue page. Consumers can depend on it like an API.
It is a central idea of data mesh, where domain teams own and publish their data as products.
terms.example: In deml-05 the model's prediction table is published as a data product with an owner and an SLA its consumers rely on.

terms.short: A large American technology company that makes Windows, Office/Microsoft 365, the Azure cloud and many business tools.
explain: Microsoft was founded in 1975 and is known for the Windows operating system and Office (Word, Excel, Outlook), now sold as Microsoft 365. Many companies run their daily work on these products.
It also runs Azure, one of the three biggest cloud platforms, and makes data products such as Microsoft Fabric and Power BI, plus GitHub and Visual Studio Code for developers.
terms.example: The Azure and Fabric labs simulate Microsoft's cloud portal and its data platform; GitHub, used in the Git labs, is also owned by Microsoft.

terms.short: Cheap object storage (such as S3) holding raw files of any format - CSV, JSON, Parquet - for later processing.
explain: A lake stores files as they are, without forcing them into tables first. It is cheap, holds any amount and any format, and many engines (Spark, Snowflake, Athena) can read it. Raw extracts usually land here first.

The risk is a 'data swamp': files nobody can find, trust or update consistently. Columnar formats and open table formats such as Delta Lake and Iceberg add structure and transactions - turning a lake into a lakehouse.
terms.example: ShopFlow lands daily order extracts in `s3://shopflow-lake/raw/orders/` before converting them to Parquet and Delta.

terms.short: A fast engine for processing large data across a cluster, used from Python, SQL or Scala; it keeps work in memory instead of writing to disk between steps.
explain: Apache Spark splits data into partitions and runs the same operation on each partition in parallel on many machines. You describe the work with DataFrames (tables in code) or SQL, and Spark builds a plan.

Nothing runs until you ask for a result (an action such as `count()` or a write). The driver program plans the job; executors on worker nodes do the work. Spark runs on YARN, Kubernetes, AWS Glue and Microsoft Fabric.
`spark-submit job.py` runs a script; the Spark UI and History Server show its jobs and stages.
terms.example: `spark.read.parquet('/silver/orders').groupBy('channel').sum('amount').show()`

terms.short: A database built for analysis: it collects cleaned data from many systems and answers large queries across years of history quickly.
explain: Operational systems - the shop database, the payment system, the CRM - each hold part of the picture and are busy serving customers. A data warehouse copies their data into one place, organised for questions like 'revenue by region per month since 2020'.

Warehouses are columnar, compressed and parallel, and are usually modelled in layers: raw data as it arrived, cleaned staging, and marts in star schemas for reporting. Snowflake, BigQuery and Redshift are cloud warehouses.
terms.example: ShopFlow's warehouse is Snowflake: RAW holds loaded data, ANALYTICS holds dbt-built marts used by the BI team.

terms.short: A Fabric mode where a semantic model reads Delta tables in OneLake directly, so reports are fast without copying data into the model.
explain: Older Power BI models either imported a copy of the data (fast but stale) or queried the source live (fresh but slow). Direct Lake reads the Delta files in OneLake straight into memory - fast and current.

Some things break it: calculated columns, SQL views and very large tables make the model fall back to slower DirectQuery, silently. Setting DirectLakeOnly makes fallback fail loudly instead. The Best Practice Analyzer lists model anti-patterns.
terms.example: With DirectLakeOnly on, a measure over a view errors instead of quietly falling back.

terms.short: An open table format that turns a folder of Parquet files into a real table with transactions, MERGE, time travel and a change log.
explain: A folder of Parquet files in a lake is not a table: two writers can collide, a failed job leaves half-written files, and there is no way to update one row. Delta Lake adds a transaction log, the `_delta_log` folder, next to the data files.

Each commit writes a numbered JSON file listing which Parquet files were added and removed. Readers use the log to see one consistent version. That makes MERGE, UPDATE and DELETE possible, lets you read an older version (time travel) and supports OPTIMIZE and VACUUM for housekeeping.
terms.example: In dewh-06 you build a Delta table from unloaded customers, MERGE a batch of changes as one commit, then read version 0 with time travel.

terms.short: Keeping data as open files in a lake while adding table features - transactions, MERGE, schema, time travel - so the lake serves warehouse work.
explain: Traditionally companies copied data from a lake into a separate warehouse, paying twice and keeping two copies in sync. A lakehouse uses open table formats (Delta Lake, Iceberg) over Parquet files so the lake itself behaves like database tables.
Data is usually organised in medallion layers: bronze (raw, replayable), silver (cleaned, deduplicated), gold (business-ready). Several engines - Spark, Flink, Snowflake - can read the same tables.
terms.example: In dedesign-02 extracts land in a bronze Delta table, are deduplicated into silver with MERGE and published to Snowflake gold.

terms.short: The language used to ask a database questions and change its data, e.g. SELECT name FROM customers.
explain: SQL (Structured Query Language) is written as short statements that read almost like English. `SELECT` reads rows, `INSERT` adds, `UPDATE` changes, `DELETE` removes, and `CREATE TABLE` defines a new table.

You say what you want, not how to find it: `SELECT name FROM customers WHERE country = 'Jordan'` - and the database decides the fastest way. Almost every database speaks SQL, with small differences between products.
terms.example: `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE country = 'Jordan';` counts the orders from Jordan - one of the first tasks in the SQL labs.
terms.analogy: Asking a librarian a precise question - 'all books by this author after 2010' - instead of searching the shelves yourself.
terms.why: SQL appears in the SQL, Django, Flask and every data lab. The ORMs in Django and Flask write SQL for you, and the labs show it.

terms.short: A set of rules that lets one program ask another program to do something.
explain: Programs do not click buttons. When one program needs something from another - the weather, a payment, a list of files - it sends a request in a format both sides agreed on. That agreed format is the API.

Most APIs today work over the web: the request is an HTTP message to a URL called an endpoint, and the answer comes back as JSON. The API hides how the other program works inside; you only need to know what to ask.
terms.example: In the Flask API lab, `GET /api/products` is an endpoint that returns the product rows as JSON, and `POST` to the same path creates a new one.
terms.analogy: A waiter in a restaurant: you never enter the kitchen, you give your order in a fixed format, and the waiter brings back the dish.
terms.why: Portals, command-line tools and scripts in these labs all call the same APIs underneath.

terms.short: The rule that every person or program gets only the permissions it needs for its job, and nothing more.
explain: If a program that only reads one folder holds administrator rights, a bug or a stolen password can destroy everything. Least privilege limits the damage: give each identity the smallest set of permissions that still lets it work.

In practice this means writing narrow policies (this bucket, read only), using roles per job instead of one shared admin account, and removing rights nobody uses. Labs make you replace 'Owner' or 'AdministratorAccess' with a precise pair of permissions.
terms.example: The pipeline role may read `s3://lake/bronze/*` and write `s3://lake/silver/*` - and is denied delete on bronze.
terms.analogy: A hotel key card that opens your room and the gym, not every door in the building.

terms.short: Role-based access control in Azure: you give an identity a role (a set of allowed actions) at a scope, and it applies to everything beneath that scope.
explain: A role assignment has three parts: who (a user, group or managed identity), which role (Reader, Contributor, Owner, or a narrow one), and where (a management group, subscription, resource group or resource).

Control-plane roles manage resources (create a storage account); data-plane roles touch the data inside (read a blob). Contributor can create a storage account but cannot read its blobs. Owner is Contributor plus the right to grant access. A deny assignment beats any role.
terms.example: Contributor on the subscription allows `Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/write` but refuses reading a blob until `Storage Blob Data Reader` is assigned.

terms.short: Access control list: an ordered list of permit and deny rules a router or firewall checks to decide which traffic may pass.
explain: Each line matches traffic by source, destination, protocol or port and says permit or deny: `access-list 101 permit tcp any host 192.168.10.20 eq 80`. The list is applied to an interface in one direction with `ip access-group 101 in`.
Two rules catch everyone. Lines are checked top to bottom and the first match wins, so order matters. And every ACL ends with an invisible `deny ip any any`, so anything not permitted is blocked.
terms.example: In the services lab you write an ACL that permits HTTP to the server and then prove the implicit deny blocks ping.

terms.short: A virtual firewall attached to an AWS server or database that lists which incoming traffic is allowed; everything else is blocked.
explain: A security group holds allow rules: 'TCP port 443 from anywhere', 'port 5432 from the app tier'. There are no deny rules - traffic not allowed is dropped.

It is stateful: if a request is allowed in, the reply is allowed back out automatically. A rule can name another security group as the source instead of an IP range, which is how a three-tier design lets only the app servers talk to the database.
terms.example: `aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id sg-1 --protocol tcp --port 22 --cidr 203.0.113.5/32` allows SSH from one address.

terms.short: An identity that Azure creates and manages for a service, so the service can sign in to other resources without anyone storing a password.
explain: Programs need credentials to call other services, and stored secrets leak. A managed identity removes the secret: Azure gives the resource an identity and hands it short-lived tokens automatically.

System-assigned identities are born and die with one resource. User-assigned identities are separate resources that several services can share and that outlive them. You give the identity a role, just like a person. Fabric's workspace identity is the same idea.
terms.example: A deployIfNotExists policy gets a managed identity with Contributor so it can actually remediate.

terms.short: The practice of understanding, sharing out and reducing a company's cloud bill, so spending is planned rather than a surprise.
explain: In the cloud anyone can create resources, and every resource costs money each hour. FinOps (finance plus operations) is how teams keep that under control.

The usual order: make spend visible (tags, cost reports by service), remove waste (stop idle servers, shrink oversized ones - 'rightsizing'), then commit to discounts for the steady baseline (Savings Plans, Reserved Instances). Budgets alert people before the bill is exceeded.
Rightsizing comes before buying discounts, or you commit to paying for capacity you do not need.
terms.example: In the FinOps lab you rightsize an oversized server first, then buy a Savings Plan sized to what is left.

terms.short: A pointer in OneLake that makes data stored elsewhere appear as a folder or table, without copying it.
explain: Copying data between teams creates duplicates that drift apart. A shortcut is like a link: a gold lakehouse can show the CMDB table that lives in another lakehouse or even in S3, and readers query it as if it were local.
Permissions of the target still apply, and deleting the shortcut does not delete the data.
terms.example: The Delta lab shares the CMDB table into gold with a shortcut instead of copying it.

terms.short: A web page made of cells of code (Python/PySpark or SQL) and their output, run against a Spark cluster - the main place data engineers write transformations.
explain: A notebook mixes code cells, results and notes. In Fabric a notebook is attached to a lakehouse and runs on Spark, so each cell can read and write large tables.

Notebooks are great for exploring but easy to make fragile: hard-coded paths, `collect()` pulling all data to one machine, full reloads every run. Production notebooks take parameters and process only new data.
terms.example: A silver notebook reads bronze incidents, keeps the latest version per `sys_id` and MERGEs into `lh_silver.incident`.

terms.short: A chain of steps that moves data from where it is produced to where it is used, cleaning and reshaping it on the way.
explain: Data starts in many places: apps, files, sensors. A pipeline collects (extracts) it, fixes and reshapes it (transforms), and stores it somewhere useful (loads) - such as a warehouse that reports read. This is called ETL, or ELT when loading comes first.
Pipelines usually run on a schedule or whenever new data arrives, and each step's output is the next step's input. When a step fails, later steps must wait, so pipelines are watched and re-run.
terms.example: Every night a pipeline copies the day's orders from the shop database, removes test orders, and loads the totals into a reporting table.
terms.analogy: A water treatment plant: water is collected, cleaned in stages and piped to homes.

terms.short: Two ways to lay out table data in files: row formats (CSV) store each record together; columnar formats (Parquet, ORC) store each column together.
explain: A CSV file stores row after row. To compute the average of one column you still read every column of every row. A columnar file stores all values of column A, then all of column B. Reading one column touches only that column's bytes.
Columnar files also compress well, because similar values sit together, and they record types. They are the right choice for analytics; row formats suit writing one record at a time.
terms.example: A query summing `amount` over a 2 GB CSV reads 2 GB; over the same data in Parquet it may read 60 MB.

terms.short: The REST API that returns rows of any ServiceNow table as JSON, page by page, used to copy tickets into a data platform.
explain: `GET /api/now/table/incident` returns incident records. Parameters shape the request: `sysparm_query` filters, `sysparm_fields` picks columns, `sysparm_limit` and `sysparm_offset` page through large tables.

For incremental loads you remember the latest `sys_updated_on` you loaded (a watermark) and next time ask only for newer rows. The API throttles heavy callers with HTTP 429, so a good pipeline retries with a pause.
terms.example: `/api/now/table/incident?sysparm_query=sys_updated_on>2026-11-01&sysparm_limit=1000&sysparm_offset=0`

terms.short: Amazon Redshift: AWS's data warehouse, a database built to run large analytical SQL queries over billions of rows.
explain: A data warehouse is a database for analysis rather than for an app's day-to-day writes. Redshift stores data in columns across many nodes so totals and joins over huge tables are fast.

Redshift Serverless sizes itself in RPUs (Redshift Processing Units). Data is loaded from S3 with `COPY`, which needs an IAM role attached to the namespace. The Data API and Query editor v2 run queries without managing connections.
terms.example: The lab creates a namespace with a load role and an 8-RPU workgroup, then COPYs clickstream JSON and orders CSV from S3.

terms.short: Data Analysis Expressions: the formula language for measures in Power BI and Fabric semantic models.
explain: A DAX measure is a calculation evaluated for whatever the report is showing - per month, per group, in total. `Incidents = COUNTROWS(fact_incident)` gives a count that changes with each filter.

`CALCULATE` changes the filters a measure is evaluated under; `DIVIDE` divides safely, returning blank instead of an error when the denominator is zero. Filtering a whole fact table with `FILTER` is slow - a simple boolean filter inside CALCULATE is usually better.
terms.example: `SLA met % = DIVIDE(CALCULATE(COUNTROWS(fact_sla), fact_sla[met] = TRUE()), COUNTROWS(fact_sla))`

terms.short: A rule that filters which rows of a table each user can see - an analyst sees only her group's incidents - applied wherever the data is queried.
explain: Giving someone access to a table normally means all of it. Row-level security adds a filter per user or role: `assignment_group = the user's group`. In a warehouse it is a T-SQL security policy; in a semantic model it is a role with a DAX filter.
Column protections sit beside it: grants on a schema, dynamic data masking that shows `j***@***.com` instead of an email, and OneLake data access roles for files.
terms.example: The security lab gives analyst Maya a role whose filter shows only incidents of the Network group.

terms.short: The way a company runs IT as a set of services for its users: requests, incidents, changes and problems handled through agreed processes.
explain: Users do not care about servers; they care that email, the shop website or payroll works. IT service management treats each of those as a service with an owner, a promised level of quality and a support process.
In practice it means a service desk, a ticketing tool such as ServiceNow, and defined processes - most often taken from ITIL - for restoring service, fixing root causes and changing systems safely.
terms.example: A failed payroll run becomes an incident on the Payroll service, worked under its SLA by the support group.

terms.short: A widely used set of best practices for IT service management; its incident, problem and change processes are the language of IT operations.
explain: ITIL describes how a well-run IT operation works. Three of its processes form a triangle. Incident management restores service as fast as possible, even with a workaround. Problem management finds and removes the root cause behind one or many incidents. Change management makes system changes safely, with the right approval.
A known error is a problem whose cause and workaround are documented. Keeping the three apart matters: restoring service is urgent, analysing why is careful, and changing production is controlled.
terms.example: Four incidents with the same symptom are linked to one problem; its fix ships as a normal change approved by the CAB.

terms.short: An unplanned interruption or reduction in the quality of a service, recorded as a ticket that is worked until service is restored.
explain: An incident is the record of 'something is broken now'. It has a number such as `INC0010021`, a short description, an affected service, an assigned group and a priority from P1 (critical) to P4 (low).

Its life: New, In Progress, On Hold (waiting on someone), Resolved, Closed. The goal is to restore service - not necessarily to find the cause; that is problem management's job. Customer-visible comments and internal work notes are different fields.
terms.example: `INC0010021` - branch network down, P1 - is acknowledged, given a customer update, and resolved inside two hours.

terms.short: How urgent a ticket is, worked out from impact (how many people or how much business is hurt) and urgency (how fast it gets worse).
explain: ITIL sets priority with a matrix. Impact: one person, a team, a whole site, all customers. Urgency: can it wait, or is it getting worse by the minute? High impact and high urgency gives P1; low and low gives P4.

Priority drives the SLA timers, so getting it wrong means the clock is wrong. When the facts change - a 'single user' problem turns out to be a whole branch - the priority must be raised, and the reason written down.
terms.example: A ticket logged as P3 for one user is re-prioritised to P1 when the whole branch is affected.

terms.short: A rota of engineers who answer alerts outside office hours, with rules that page the next person if the first does not respond.
explain: A 24/7 service needs someone reachable at 3 am. The on-call rota names a primary and a secondary - two different people - for each shift. An alert pages the primary first.

An escalation policy says how long to wait before paging the next step. It is designed backwards from the SLA: if pick-up must happen in 15 minutes, the primary cannot have all 15. At the end of a shift a hand-over tells the next team what is still open.
terms.example: Page primary, wait 5 minutes, page secondary, wait 5 minutes, page the duty manager - all inside the 15-minute pick-up SLA.

terms.short: A written, machine-checkable agreement between a data producer and its consumers about a dataset's schema, meaning, quality rules and delivery promises.
explain: Consumers build reports on a table; the producing team changes a column and everything breaks. A data contract makes the expectations explicit: the fields and types, which are required, quality rules (no negative amounts), an SLA (fresh by 06:00) and an owner.

Contracts are versioned with semantic versioning. Adding an optional field is a minor change; renaming or removing one is breaking and needs a new major version, so consumers can move at their own pace. Tools validate the live data against the contract.
terms.example: In dequality-04 a column rename sold as minor release 1.3.0 is refused; accepted as 2.0.0 it is published to the catalogue.

terms.short: A searchable inventory of an organisation's datasets with descriptions, owners, domains, tags, classifications and lineage.
explain: A catalogue answers 'is there a table for this, which one is right, and who do I ask?'. It ingests technical metadata automatically (schemas, column types, lineage, usage) and lets people add business context: descriptions, owners, a domain such as Sales, tags such as PII.
A dataset with an owner and documentation is one someone is accountable for; a dataset nobody owns is one nobody should build on.
terms.example: In dequality-06 you give the orders mart a Sales domain, an owner, a PII tag and a description in DataHub.

track.tagline: Rent servers, storage, networks and databases from Amazon, and control them from the command line.
what: AWS is the cloud business of Amazon and the largest cloud provider in the world. Instead of buying computers, a company opens an AWS account and rents what it needs - a virtual server, a storage bucket, a database - paying by the hour or by the gigabyte.

This track covers the core building blocks every AWS engineer uses: S3 for files, EC2 for servers, VPC for networks, IAM for permissions, Lambda for code without servers, and DynamoDB and RDS for databases.
how: Everything in AWS is a resource in an account and a region, created through one API. The web console, the `aws` CLI and infrastructure-as-code tools all call that API, so what you do in one shows in the others.
Security is deny-by-default: an identity can only do what an IAM policy allows. Networking is private by default: nothing reaches a server in your VPC until a route and a security group allow it.
track.who: Beginners in cloud computing, developers deploying their first application, and anyone preparing for an AWS associate certification.
learn: Drive AWS from the CLI and read its JSON answers with --query
Create buckets and objects and understand global bucket names
Design a VPC with public and private subnets across zones
Launch, tag, stop and terminate EC2 instances
Write trust and permission policies and diagnose AccessDenied
Choose between DynamoDB and RDS and assemble a three-tier architecture
before: How to type commands in a terminal
What an IP address and a port are
track.simulated: The AWS account is simulated: the CLI and console change a model of AWS resources with realistic ids, errors and rules, but nothing is billed and no real servers start.

terms.short: Renting computers, storage and services from a provider over the internet instead of buying and running your own.
explain: Running your own servers means buying hardware, a room to keep it in, power, cooling and staff. A cloud provider has huge data centres and rents small pieces of them to anyone, by the minute or by the gigabyte.

You create things - a virtual machine, a database, a storage bucket - with a few clicks in a web portal or one command, and delete them when you are done. The big providers are Amazon (AWS), Microsoft (Azure) and Google (Google Cloud).
terms.example: In the cloud labs, a command such as creating a storage bucket takes seconds - in a company before the cloud, getting a new server could take weeks.
terms.analogy: Using electricity from the grid instead of building your own power station: you plug in and pay for what you use.

terms.short: Amazon Web Services: Amazon's cloud, where companies rent servers, storage, databases and networks by the hour instead of buying hardware.
explain: AWS is the cloud business of Amazon. Instead of buying computers and putting them in a building, a company opens an AWS account and rents what it needs: a virtual server, a storage bucket, a database. It pays only while the thing exists.

AWS offers over two hundred services. Each has a short name - S3 for storage, EC2 for servers, IAM for permissions. Everything lives in an account, inside a region (a group of data centres in one part of the world).
You can drive AWS three ways: the web console (clicking), the `aws` command line tool, or code that calls its API. All three do the same work.
terms.example: In the labs, `aws sts get-caller-identity` asks AWS which account and user you are, and `aws s3 mb s3://my-bucket` creates storage.
terms.analogy: Like renting a fully equipped flat by the night instead of building a house: someone else owns the building, you pay for the rooms you use.
terms.why: Many labs here - AWS, Cloud Operations, Cloud Data Platform, Terraform - run against a simulated AWS account.

terms.short: The `aws` program you type commands into to control AWS from a terminal, instead of clicking in the web console.
explain: The AWS CLI is a command line program. Every command has the same shape: `aws <service> <operation> --options`, for example `aws ec2 describe-instances`. It sends the request to AWS and prints the answer.

The answer is JSON by default. Two flags make it useful in scripts: `--output text|table|json` changes the format, and `--query` picks out only the fields you want, using a small query language called JMESPath.
terms.example: `aws s3api list-buckets --query "Buckets[].Name" --output text` prints just the bucket names, one per line.
terms.analogy: A phone line to AWS where you speak in short fixed sentences instead of pointing at things on a screen.
terms.why: Most lab tasks are written as `aws` commands; reading the JSON it returns is how you find ids to use in the next command.

terms.short: A geographic area, such as Ireland or Virginia, where a cloud provider has data centres; every resource you create lives in one region.
explain: A cloud is not one place. AWS and Azure each run data centres in dozens of areas of the world, called regions. AWS names them like `eu-west-1`; Azure names them like `westeurope`.

When you create a server or a bucket you choose a region. The data stays there, the price depends on it, and users near it get faster answers. Some laws require data about citizens to stay inside a given region.
A few services are global and not tied to a region - for example IAM on AWS - which matters when you write rules that block regions.
terms.example: `az group create --name rg-lab --location westeurope` puts a resource group in the West Europe region.
terms.why: Labs ask you to pick locations, spread subnets across zones and write region guardrails - all of it starts from knowing what a region is.

terms.short: A storage container in Amazon S3 that holds any number of files (called objects), each reached by a key such as `reports/2026/jan.csv`.
explain: Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service) stores files - photos, logs, CSV exports, backups - without you managing disks. You create a bucket and put objects into it. An object is the file plus a little metadata, and its key is its full name.

Bucket names are global: no two AWS accounts in the world can have the same bucket name, and the name must be lowercase and DNS-safe because it becomes part of a web address. A bucket must be empty before it can be deleted.
Buckets also carry settings: versioning, encryption, lifecycle rules, and policies saying who may read them.
terms.example: `aws s3 mb s3://selfstudy-lab-yourname` creates a bucket; `aws s3 cp notes.txt s3://selfstudy-lab-yourname/` uploads a file.
terms.analogy: A huge cloakroom: you hand in a coat (the file), get a ticket with a unique name (the key), and the building looks after it.
terms.why: S3 is the first AWS service in the labs and the base of every data lake in the cloud data platform labs.

terms.short: A Virtual Private Cloud: your own isolated private network inside AWS, where your servers and databases get their IP addresses.
explain: When you put servers in AWS they need a network. A VPC is that network: you give it an address range such as `10.0.0.0/16`, then divide it into subnets, add route tables saying where traffic goes, and gateways to reach the internet.

Nothing reaches a resource in your VPC from outside unless you open a path on purpose. Every account comes with a default VPC; real projects build their own. A VPC cannot be deleted while it still contains subnets or other resources.
terms.example: `aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.0.0.0/16` creates the network; subnets and security groups are then created inside it.
terms.analogy: A private office floor in a shared skyscraper: you decide the room layout, the locks, and which doors lead to the street.

terms.short: A virtual server you rent from AWS: you pick a size and a disk image, and AWS starts a machine you can log in to.
explain: EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) gives you virtual machines called instances. You choose an instance type (how much CPU and memory, for example `t3.micro`), an AMI (the disk image with the operating system), a subnet to place it in, and a key pair for logging in.
An instance can be stopped (shut down, disk kept, little cost) and started again, or terminated (deleted for good). Mixing those up is a classic mistake. Each instance gets an id like `i-0abc123`.
terms.example: `aws ec2 run-instances --image-id ami-123 --instance-type t3.micro --key-name lab-key` launches a server.
terms.analogy: Renting a computer in a data centre that you control remotely: you choose its size and software, and give it back when done.

terms.short: AWS Identity and Access Management: the service that decides who (which user, role or program) may do what on which AWS resource.
explain: Every request to AWS is signed by an identity. IAM holds those identities - users (people or programs with long-term keys), groups, and roles (identities that are borrowed for a while) - and the policies that grant them permissions.

By default everything is denied. A request succeeds only if some policy allows it and no policy explicitly denies it. When a call fails with `AccessDenied`, the cause is always a missing allow or a deny somewhere.
IAM is global: it is not tied to a region.
terms.example: `aws iam create-role --role-name lambda-exec --assume-role-policy-document file://trust.json` creates a role.

terms.short: A virtual firewall attached to an AWS server or database that lists which incoming traffic is allowed; everything else is blocked.
explain: A security group holds allow rules: 'TCP port 443 from anywhere', 'port 5432 from the app tier'. There are no deny rules - traffic not allowed is dropped.

It is stateful: if a request is allowed in, the reply is allowed back out automatically. A rule can name another security group as the source instead of an IP range, which is how a three-tier design lets only the app servers talk to the database.
terms.example: `aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id sg-1 --protocol tcp --port 22 --cidr 203.0.113.5/32` allows SSH from one address.

terms.short: A piece of code that AWS runs for you when something triggers it, with no server for you to manage; you pay only while it runs.
explain: AWS Lambda is 'serverless' computing. You upload a function - a few lines of Python or JavaScript - and say what starts it: an HTTP call, a file landing in S3, a schedule. AWS starts a runtime, runs your code, and stops it.

Every function runs as an IAM role, its execution role. If the role lacks a permission, the call fails with `AccessDenied`. Output and errors go to CloudWatch Logs, which also needs a permission - the basic execution policy.
terms.example: The IAM lab creates a function with `--role <role ARN>`, invokes it, gets AccessDenied, attaches the basic execution policy, and invokes again.

terms.short: A slice of a cloud network's address range (one availability zone on AWS); servers and databases are placed in subnets.
explain: A VPC (or an Azure VNet) is cut into subnets, each with its own smaller CIDR range. On AWS each subnet is in exactly one availability zone. Every server or database is created in a subnet.

On AWS a subnet is 'public' only because its route table sends `0.0.0.0/0` (all other addresses) to an internet gateway. A 'private' subnet has no such route; its servers reach the internet only through a NAT gateway, and nobody can reach them from outside. Web servers in public subnets and databases in private ones is the classic layout.
terms.example: `aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id vpc-1 --cidr-block 10.0.1.0/24 --availability-zone eu-west-1a`

terms.short: A block of IP addresses that forms one network; the mask, such as /24, says how many leading bits are the network part.
explain: `192.168.10.10/24` means the first 24 bits (`192.168.10`) are the network and the last 8 bits are the host. The mask can also be written `255.255.255.0`. Hosts in the same subnet talk directly; to reach another subnet they go through a router.

Each subnet has a network address (first), a broadcast address (last) and usable host addresses between them. For `/26` the block size is 256 - 192 = 64, so `10.20.30.45/26` is in `10.20.30.0`-`.63`: network `.0`, broadcast `.63`, hosts `.1`-`.62`.
terms.example: The addressing lab breaks a ping on purpose by giving one host `/25` and the other `/24` - a mask mismatch, which is not symmetrical.

terms.short: Amazon is a large online retailer; AWS (Amazon Web Services) is its cloud business, the biggest cloud provider in the world.
explain: Amazon began as an online bookshop and became one of the largest companies in the world. To run its own huge website it built enormous data centres, and in 2006 it began renting that capacity to others as Amazon Web Services (AWS).
AWS now offers hundreds of services: virtual machines (EC2), storage (S3), databases, networking, AI and more, in regions across the world. Many start-ups and large companies run entirely on AWS.
terms.example: The AWS labs simulate the AWS Management Console and CLI, where commands such as `aws s3 mb` create resources in a region.

terms.short: A way of writing a range of IP addresses as one address plus a size, like `10.0.0.0/16`, used to size networks and subnets.
explain: Every machine on a network needs an IP address. When you build a cloud network you reserve a whole range at once. CIDR notation writes that range as a starting address and a slash number.

The number after the slash says how many leading bits are fixed. `/16` fixes 16 bits and leaves about 65,000 addresses; `/24` leaves 256. A subnet must sit inside its network's range, and two networks you want to connect must not overlap - Azure and AWS refuse overlapping ranges.
terms.analogy: Like a street with house numbers 1-256: the street is the network, and you hand out blocks of numbers to each building (subnet).

terms.short: A number that identifies a computer on a network, so data can be delivered to it.
explain: Every device on a network needs an address. An IPv4 address is four numbers from 0 to 255 separated by dots, such as `192.168.10.10`. IPv6 is a newer, much longer format with letters and colons.

Part of the address names the network and part names the device inside it; the subnet mask (the `/24` after the address) says where the split is. Addresses starting with `10.`, `172.16-31.` and `192.168.` are private: used inside homes and companies, never directly on the internet.
terms.example: In the networking lab you give two PCs `192.168.10.10/24` and `192.168.10.11/24`; because the first three numbers match, they are on the same network and can ping each other.
terms.analogy: A street address: the street name is the network part, the house number is the device part.

terms.short: A link between two Azure virtual networks so resources in each can reach the other privately; it must be created from both sides.
explain: A peering is really two objects: one on network A pointing at B, and one on B pointing at A. With only one side, the state is `Initiated`; it becomes `Connected` only when both exist.

Flags control what can cross: `allowForwardedTraffic` lets traffic that a hub firewall forwarded in, `allowGatewayTransit` (on the hub) and `useRemoteGateways` (on the spoke) share a VPN gateway. Putting a flag on the wrong side is a common error. Peering is not transitive.
terms.example: After `az network vnet peering create` on the spoke only, the state reads Initiated; adding the hub side makes it Connected.

terms.short: One or more separate data centres inside a region, with their own power and network, so a failure in one does not stop the others.
