explain: A region is split into availability zones (AZs), usually three. Each zone is a physically separate building or group of buildings, a few kilometres from the others, with its own power and cooling.

If you put two copies of your application in two zones, a fire or power cut in one zone does not take you down. That is why lab tasks ask for subnets 'in different zones'. On AWS zones are named by adding a letter: `eu-west-1a`, `eu-west-1b`.
terms.example: In the VPC lab you create one subnet in `eu-west-1a` and one in `eu-west-1b`.

terms.short: Designing a system so it keeps working even when one of its parts fails.
explain: Any single machine, disk or network link will fail one day. A highly available system has no single point of failure: it runs spare copies, so when one breaks another takes over (failover), often automatically.

Availability is measured as the percentage of time a service works: 99.9% allows about 9 hours of downtime a year, 99.99% about 53 minutes. Clouds help by offering separate data centres (availability zones) in each region.
terms.example: A database with a standby copy in a second availability zone keeps serving the app when the first zone loses power.
terms.analogy: A plane with two engines: if one stops, the other keeps it flying.

terms.short: A small language, used by the AWS CLI's `--query` flag, for picking a few fields out of a large JSON answer.
explain: AWS answers often hold hundreds of lines of JSON. You usually need one value: an id, a name, an address. JMESPath is a way to point at that value.

`Buckets[].Name` means: take the list called Buckets, and from every item take Name. `length(Buckets)` counts them. `Reservations[0].Instances[0].InstanceId` walks down to one id. Combine it with `--output text` and the result can go straight into a script variable.
terms.example: `aws rds describe-db-instances --query "DBInstances[0].Endpoint.Address" --output text` prints only the database address.

terms.short: Amazon Relational Database Service: AWS runs a SQL database (PostgreSQL, MySQL and others) for you, with backups and patching included.
explain: RDS gives you a ready relational database. You choose the engine, the size and the subnets; AWS installs it, patches it and backs it up. You connect to it with a normal database client using its endpoint, a host name AWS gives you.
Multi-AZ keeps a standby copy in a second availability zone and fails over to it automatically. RDS only offers the engines AWS supports - asking for another engine is refused.
terms.example: `aws rds describe-db-instances --query "DBInstances[0].Endpoint.Address"` finds the host name to connect to.

terms.short: A list of rules that says, for each destination address range, where network traffic leaving a subnet should go next.
explain: Each subnet is linked to a route table. Every line says 'traffic for this CIDR goes to this target': the local network, an internet gateway, a NAT gateway, a Transit Gateway, a VPN or a firewall.

When several lines match, the most specific one (longest prefix, e.g. /24 beats /16) wins. A missing route - often the return route - is a frequent cause of 'it works one way only'. Azure has the same idea, called user-defined routes.
terms.example: A private route table holds `10.0.0.0/16 -> local` and `0.0.0.0/0 -> nat-123`.

terms.short: A gateway that lets servers in a private subnet reach the internet (for updates) while nothing on the internet can reach them.
explain: An internet gateway (IGW) connects a VPC to the internet in both directions. A NAT gateway is one-way: private servers send traffic out through it, it swaps their private address for its own public one, and only replies come back.
NAT gateways charge per gigabyte. Sending large S3 traffic through one is a well-known waste; an S3 gateway endpoint carries that traffic for free.
terms.example: Private route table: `0.0.0.0/0 -> nat-0abc`, while the NAT gateway itself sits in a public subnet.

terms.short: The worldwide network that connects billions of computers so they can send data to each other.
explain: The internet is many smaller networks - homes, companies, universities, data centres - joined together by routers that pass data along. No single company owns it.

Data travels in small pieces called packets. Each packet carries the address of the computer it is going to (its IP address), and routers forward it hop by hop until it arrives. The web, email and video calls are all services that run on top of the internet.
terms.example: In the Wireshark lab, loading neverssl.com sends packets from the laptop through the home router out to the internet and back.
terms.analogy: The postal system: letters (packets) carry an address and are passed from sorting office to sorting office until they reach the door.

terms.short: A network device that connects different networks and forwards packets between them by their destination IP address.
explain: A switch connects devices inside one network; a router connects networks to each other - your home network to your internet provider, or one company VLAN to another. Each router interface has an IP address in the network it touches.

For each packet the router reads the destination IP, looks it up in its routing table, and sends it out of the best interface toward the next hop. A host sends anything not on its own network to its default gateway, which is a router.
terms.example: The routing lab builds three routers in a line; the two ends can reach each other only after the routers know routes to every network.

terms.short: Deciding what an identified user or program is allowed to do, such as read a file but not delete it.
explain: Once a system knows who you are (authentication), it checks your permissions: rules that say which actions you may take on which things. A student may read a course; only a teacher may change grades.

Good practice is least privilege: give each user or program only the permissions it really needs. On Linux, file permissions decide who may read, write or run each file; clouds use roles and policies.
terms.example: In the Linux permissions lab, `chmod 600 secret.txt` authorises only the file's owner to read and write it - everyone else is refused.
terms.analogy: Your ID gets you into the building; your key card decides which rooms open for you.

terms.short: Transmission Control Protocol: a reliable way to send data, which numbers every byte, confirms delivery and re-sends what is lost.
explain: IP delivers packets but promises nothing: they can be lost, duplicated or arrive out of order. TCP runs on top and turns that into a reliable stream. It first opens a connection (the three-way handshake), numbers the data, and the receiver acknowledges what arrived.
Missing pieces are sent again and everything is put back in order. HTTP, HTTPS, SSH and database connections all use TCP. The cost is a little extra delay and overhead compared with UDP.
terms.example: Following the TCP stream of the web request in Lab 1 shows the whole HTTP conversation rebuilt from many TCP segments.

terms.short: A number from 0 to 65535 that says which program on a computer should receive a piece of network traffic.
explain: One computer runs many network programs at once. The IP address gets data to the right computer; the port number gets it to the right program on that computer.

Well-known services use fixed ports: 80 for HTTP, 443 for HTTPS, 22 for SSH, 53 for DNS, 5432 for PostgreSQL. A program that waits for connections is said to listen on a port. Development servers often use 3000, 5000 or 8000.
terms.example: `http://localhost:5000` means: this same computer, port 5000 - which is where the Flask development server listens in the Flask labs.
terms.analogy: A flat number in an apartment building: the street address finds the building, the flat number finds the right door.

terms.short: A line in .claude/settings.json that allows, asks about or denies one tool on one target, such as Bash(git diff:*) or Read(.env).
explain: Rules are standing decisions, checked into the repo and reviewed like code. Each rule names a tool and a specifier: for `Bash` it is a command PREFIX ending in `:*` (`Bash(git push:*)`); for file tools it is a path GLOB (`Edit(src/**)`). A rule with the wrong syntax matches nothing and fails silently.

The order is fixed: deny first, then ask, then allow. Deny beats every mode, even bypassPermissions. Settings files at several levels - user, project, local - are merged; `claude permissions` shows the merged result and which file each rule came from.
terms.example: `"deny": ["Bash(rm:*)", "Read(.env)"]` stops a delete and keeps the secrets file unreadable whatever mode is active.

terms.short: A large American technology company that makes Windows, Office/Microsoft 365, the Azure cloud and many business tools.
explain: Microsoft was founded in 1975 and is known for the Windows operating system and Office (Word, Excel, Outlook), now sold as Microsoft 365. Many companies run their daily work on these products.
It also runs Azure, one of the three biggest cloud platforms, and makes data products such as Microsoft Fabric and Power BI, plus GitHub and Visual Studio Code for developers.
terms.example: The Azure and Fabric labs simulate Microsoft's cloud portal and its data platform; GitHub, used in the Git labs, is also owned by Microsoft.

terms.short: Google's cloud platform, which rents out computing, storage, data and AI services.
explain: Google runs some of the largest computer networks in the world for Search, YouTube and Gmail. Google Cloud Platform (GCP) rents parts of that infrastructure to companies.
It offers virtual machines, Kubernetes (which Google created), the BigQuery data warehouse and the Vertex AI platform. With AWS and Microsoft Azure it is one of the three largest cloud providers.
terms.example: A company might store its data in BigQuery and train models with Vertex AI - both Google Cloud services.

terms.short: A complete pretend computer running as a program inside a real computer, with its own operating system.
explain: One powerful physical server can be split into many virtual machines (VMs). Special software called a hypervisor gives each VM a share of the real processor, memory and disk, and each one boots its own operating system.
To the software inside, a VM looks like a real machine. Clouds rent VMs by the minute. They are heavier than containers, because each VM carries a whole operating system.
terms.example: Renting a Linux VM in a cloud gives you a machine with an IP address you can log into with SSH, though no physical box was set up for you.
terms.analogy: Flats in one building: each has its own door, kitchen and furniture, but they share the same walls and foundations.

terms.short: How well a system keeps working when much more work arrives, by adding more resources.
explain: A website with 10 users and one server might get 10,000 users tomorrow. A scalable system handles that by growing. Scaling up (vertically) means a bigger machine; scaling out (horizontally) means more machines sharing the load.
Scaling out needs a design where any copy can serve any request, usually behind a load balancer, with data kept in a shared database. Clouds can add and remove copies automatically - autoscaling.
terms.example: When traffic doubles, a scaled-out web app simply runs four copies instead of two behind its load balancer.
terms.analogy: A supermarket opening more checkout lanes when the queue gets long.

terms.short: A way of using a program by typing text commands instead of clicking buttons.
explain: A command-line interface (CLI) reads a line you type, does it, and prints the result as text. `git status`, `kubectl get pods` and `python manage.py migrate` are all CLI commands: a program name, then words and flags telling it what to do.

A CLI looks harder than a graphical interface at first, but it is faster for experts, it can be written into scripts, and it does exactly the same in every environment. Many cloud products offer both a portal and a CLI that call the same API.
terms.example: In the Django labs, `python manage.py makemigrations` is Django's CLI: no window opens, it reads your models and prints which migration it created.
terms.analogy: Giving instructions to an assistant in short exact sentences instead of pointing at things.

terms.short: A plain-text format for data, made of names and values in curly braces, that almost every program can read.
explain: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) writes data as text. An object is `{"name": "Mug", "price": 8.5}` - names in double quotes, a colon, then a value. A list is `[1, 2, 3]`. Values can be text, numbers, `true`/`false`, `null`, objects or lists.

Because it is simple text, any language can produce and read it. That is why APIs send JSON, and why many configuration files and saved records use it. A missing comma or quote makes the whole document invalid.
terms.example: The Flask API lab returns `[{"id": 1, "name": "Fedora", "price": 39.5}]` - a JSON list of objects, one per database row.
terms.analogy: A labelled form: every box has a printed label (the name) and something written in it (the value).

terms.short: A set of rules that lets one program ask another program to do something.
explain: Programs do not click buttons. When one program needs something from another - the weather, a payment, a list of files - it sends a request in a format both sides agreed on. That agreed format is the API.

Most APIs today work over the web: the request is an HTTP message to a URL called an endpoint, and the answer comes back as JSON. The API hides how the other program works inside; you only need to know what to ask.
terms.example: In the Flask API lab, `GET /api/products` is an endpoint that returns the product rows as JSON, and `POST` to the same path creates a new one.
terms.analogy: A waiter in a restaurant: you never enter the kitchen, you give your order in a fixed format, and the waiter brings back the dish.
terms.why: Portals, command-line tools and scripts in these labs all call the same APIs underneath.

terms.short: Microsoft Azure: Microsoft's cloud, where companies rent virtual machines, storage, networks, databases and managed services.
explain: Azure is Microsoft's public cloud, the main rival to AWS. A company signs up, gets a subscription (a billing and access boundary) and creates resources in it: virtual machines, storage accounts, networks, web apps, Kubernetes clusters.
Every resource lives in a resource group and a region. Azure Resource Manager (ARM) is the single API behind everything: the Azure portal, the `az` CLI, templates and Terraform all call it.
Many companies choose Azure because they already use Microsoft products such as Windows Server, Office and Entra ID for staff sign-in.
terms.example: `az group create --name rg-lab --location westeurope` then `az vm create ...` builds a virtual machine in that group.
terms.analogy: The same idea as AWS from a different landlord: you rent building blocks of computing by the hour.
terms.why: The Azure, Azure Architecture and Terraform labs run against a simulated Azure subscription.

terms.short: The delay between asking for something and starting to get the answer, usually measured in milliseconds.
explain: Every request takes time: the data travels over the network, waits in queues, and is processed. Latency is that wait. A web page with 50 ms latency feels instant; 2 seconds feels slow.

Distance, slow disks, too many round trips and busy servers all add latency. Caching, putting servers closer to users, indexes and fewer requests reduce it. Latency is different from bandwidth, which is how much data per second can flow.
terms.example: `ping` prints a time for each reply, such as `time=12 ms` - that is the round-trip latency to the other host.
terms.analogy: The time between pressing a doorbell and the door opening, regardless of how many people then walk out.

terms.short: Rules that move S3 files to cheaper, slower storage as they age, delete them when no longer needed, and keep old versions for undo.
explain: S3 has several storage classes. Standard is fast and the most expensive per gigabyte. Standard-IA (infrequent access) and Glacier are cheaper to store but charge to read and have minimum storage times - Standard-IA needs at least 30 days.

A lifecycle rule automates moves: 'after 30 days go to IA, after 90 days to Glacier, after 365 days delete'. Versioning keeps every older copy of an object when it is overwritten or deleted, so a bad data load can be undone.
terms.example: The data lake lab sets landing data to move to Standard-IA at 30 days, Glacier Instant Retrieval at 90, and expire at 365.

terms.short: A JSON document listing which actions (like `s3:GetObject`) are allowed or denied on which resources, attached to a user, group or role.
explain: A policy has statements. Each statement has an Effect (Allow or Deny), Actions (`s3:PutObject`), Resources (an ARN such as `arn:aws:s3:::lake/silver/*`) and optional Conditions.

A trust policy is a special kind attached to a role: its Principal says who may assume the role. Permission policies say what the role may do. An explicit Deny anywhere always beats an Allow. The IAM policy simulator lets you test a policy before running anything.
terms.example: `{"Effect":"Allow","Action":"s3:GetObject","Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::lake/bronze/*"}`

terms.short: A managed encryption key, kept inside a cloud key service (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault) that encrypts data for you and logs every use.
explain: Encrypting data needs a key, and the key must not sit next to the data. A key service keeps keys in protected hardware; services such as S3 ask it to encrypt and decrypt, and your program never sees the raw key.

A customer managed key has a key policy saying who may use it. Removing the line that delegates to IAM can lock everyone out. Azure Key Vault plays the same role and also stores secrets such as passwords, so code reads them at run time.
terms.example: The lake lab sets bucket default encryption to SSE-KMS with the key `alias/shopflow-lake` and a Bucket Key to cut KMS calls.

terms.short: An Amazon Machine Image: a saved disk image (operating system plus software) that new EC2 instances start from.
explain: Every EC2 instance boots from an AMI. AWS publishes AMIs for Linux and Windows; companies build their own 'golden AMIs' that already contain security hardening, patches and agents.

EC2 Image Builder automates this: a recipe lists components (update, harden, test), a pipeline builds a new AMI on a schedule, and the new image is rolled into Auto Scaling groups. Servers are then replaced with fresh ones instead of being patched by hand.
terms.example: `aws ec2 describe-images --owners amazon` lists AMIs you can launch; the golden AMI lab builds one with Image Builder.

terms.short: An AWS identity with permissions that a service, program or person can borrow for a short time, instead of holding a permanent password.
explain: A role is not a person. It is a set of permissions plus a trust policy that says who may assume it - for example 'the Lambda service' or 'the Glue service'. When assumed, AWS hands out temporary credentials that expire on their own.

Because nothing long-lived is stored, roles are safer than access keys. A role has two separate documents: the trust policy (who may wear it) and permission policies (what it may do). Mixing those up is the classic mistake.
terms.example: A Lambda function runs as role `lambda-exec`; until `AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole` is attached it cannot write its logs.

terms.short: An Amazon Resource Name: the full, unique address of one AWS resource, written like `arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/lambda-exec`.
explain: Inside one service a resource has a short name, but policies and other services need to point at it exactly. The ARN is that exact address.

It is built from parts separated by colons: `arn`, partition (`aws`), service (`iam`, `s3`), region, account id, and the resource path. Some parts are empty for global services - an S3 bucket ARN has no region or account: `arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket`.
terms.example: `aws lambda create-function --role arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/lambda-exec ...` needs the role's ARN, not its name.

terms.short: The rule that every person or program gets only the permissions it needs for its job, and nothing more.
explain: If a program that only reads one folder holds administrator rights, a bug or a stolen password can destroy everything. Least privilege limits the damage: give each identity the smallest set of permissions that still lets it work.

In practice this means writing narrow policies (this bucket, read only), using roles per job instead of one shared admin account, and removing rights nobody uses. Labs make you replace 'Owner' or 'AdministratorAccess' with a precise pair of permissions.
terms.example: The pipeline role may read `s3://lake/bronze/*` and write `s3://lake/silver/*` - and is denied delete on bronze.
terms.analogy: A hotel key card that opens your room and the gym, not every door in the building.
